meta.blurb: Kofi has a bad case of hiccups in a museum, and a fossil scientist says even hiccups have a story. As they walk, he learns that his jaw, ear bones and hands trace back to ancient fish.
meta.bible:
Kofi: a ten-year-old boy with a bad case of the hiccups, curious and a little funny. Dr Adjoa: a kind fossil scientist who works at the Museum of Natural History and loves bones. They walk through the museum halls in one afternoon, from the Fish Hall to the Hall of Mammals. Key terms: Fossil, Fossils, Vertebrate, Vertebrates, Backbone, Skull, Skeleton, Gill, Gills, Arch, Arches, Jaw, Jaws, Lamprey, Shark, Sharks, Denticles, Embryo, Embryos, Fin, Fins, Limb, Limbs, Humerus, Radius, Ulna, Tiktaalik, Tetrapod, Tetrapods, Acanthostega, Amphibian, Amphibians, Reptile, Reptiles, Mammal, Mammals, Lung, Lungs, Lungfish, Swim bladder, Nerve, Nerves, Laryngeal, Giraffe, Hox, Zebrafish, Pax6, Cones, Primates, Receptors, Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup, Eardrum, Goosebumps, Hiccups, Tadpole, Tadpoles, Coccyx, Yolk, Evolution, Ancestor, Ancestors, Radioactive, Cambrian, Devonian, Haeckel, Fish Hall. Facts: the first animals with backbones were small fish-like creatures more than 500 million years ago; Tiktaalik lived about 375 million years ago and its fossils come from Arctic Canada; the first four-legged animals appear about 365 million years ago; about seven in ten human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish; humans have about 400 working smell genes. Where scientists are not sure, the text says so, especially for the cause of Hiccups. Voice: playful, clear and wondering; the science is real and hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes. Kofi's mother: dropped him at the museum and will collect him at closing time. The museum's halls run from oldest to newest, so the stairs go down to the oldest animals. Dr Adjoa's notebook has three rules: ask what a thing is, ask how we know, and say so when nobody is sure. Kofi and Dr Adjoa made a bet at the start: she promises to come back to the hiccups before closing time. Key terms (more): Vertebra, Vertebrae, Discs.
Galápagos: a group of islands where scientists measured finch beaks during a drought. Hall of Clues: the first room on the way down, with a cabinet of rocks, bones, shells and a brass microscope. DNA: the instruction book inside cells. Beetles, Finches, Beaks.
Hall of Time: the second room, with fossils and a long strip of cloth where each step is a hundred million years. The Earth is about four and a half billion years old. Key terms (more): Mineral, Minerals, Layers, Volcanic, Ash, Half-life, Geologists, Atoms.
Fish Hall: the third room, where the first fish and the lamprey tank are. Cambrian: the period more than five hundred million years ago. Chengjiang: a site in China with fossils about 520 million years old. Key terms (more): Chordate, Chordates, Notochord, Lancelet, Cartilage, Invertebrates, Skull, Spine, Backbone, Armour, Jawless, Ecosystems. A human has seven neck bones, like a giraffe.
Dunkleosteus: an armoured jawed fish that lived about 370 million years ago; its jaws had sharp bone edges instead of teeth. Spiracle: a shark's small breathing hole behind the eye, from the first gill slit. Key terms (more): Hinge, Gill arch, Spiracle, Ears.
Key terms (more): Enamel, Dentine, Conveyor, Sandpaper, Rays, Bony fish, Cartilaginous. An adult human has about 206 bones; a baby has more separate pieces.
Hall of Beginnings: a room of embryo models. A human embryo has folds called arches on its neck in its first weeks; it never breathes with them; it gets oxygen from its mother's blood. Key terms (more): Umbilical, Accordion, Chambers, Valves, Arteries, Warm-blooded.
Key terms (more): Hiccup, Phrenic, Vagus (Latin for wandering), Diaphragm, Gill cover, Reflex, Cranial. People have twelve pairs of nerves that leave the brain. The nerve to the voice box loops under the great artery near the heart; in a giraffe the detour is very long. The diaphragm starts near the neck in the embryo and moves down, so its nerve starts in the neck.
Bichir: an African river fish with gills and simple lungs. Key terms (more): Epiglottis, Windpipe, Swim bladder, Air sacs, Lungfish, Bichir, Hall.
Key terms (more): Lateral line, Hair cells, Otoliths, Retina, Lens, Cones, Pores, Goldfish, Octopus. Humans have about 400 working smell genes and many hundreds more that no longer work. Hair cells in the lateral line and the inner ear are the same kind of cell; fish, amphibians and birds can regrow them but mammals mostly cannot.
Key terms (more): Coelacanth (a lobe-finned fish found alive in 1938 off South Africa, thought extinct with the dinosaurs), Lobe-finned, Ray fins, Radius, Ulna, Carpals, Bat, Whale, Horse, Mole. The hand begins as a paddle in the embryo; the fingers appear when cells between them die away.
Flipper, Flippers.
Hall of Shores: a hall with a model of a Devonian river bank about 400 million years ago; the Devonian is sometimes called the Age of Fishes. Gallery of In-Betweens: the room with the Tiktaalik cast. Key terms (more): Mudskipper, Mudskippers, Millipedes, Eurypterid, Shore, Floodplains, Devonian. Giant sea scorpions lived in Devonian waters and could grow longer than a man.
Tiktaalik: the name is Inuktitut for a large freshwater fish; it was chosen with elders of Nunavut, the Canadian territory where the fossils were found. In its time that place was warm and green. Key terms (more): Inuktitut, Nunavut, Canadian, Arctic, Crocodile, Shoulder girdle, Push-up, Girdle.
Acanthostega: an early four-legged animal from Greenland about 365 million years old; eight fingers on each front foot; it kept gills; its limbs were too weak for land and were probably used in water. Ichthyostega: another early tetrapod from Greenland with seven toes on each back foot. Zachelmie: in 2010 scientists reported four-limbed tracks from Poland, nearly 400 million years old, older than Tiktaalik; scientists still discuss them. Key terms (more): Greenland, Poland, Salamander, Tracks, Sparrow, Dinosaur, Dinosaurs, Hips, Pelvis. The first four-legged animals known from skeletons are about 365 million years old.
Gene Gallery: a room of glowing screens about genes. A gene is a short stretch of DNA that works like a recipe; a human has about twenty thousand genes. Hox genes lay out the body from head to tail and sit along the DNA in the same order as the body parts they control. Pax6 starts eye building in flies, fish, mice and people. Key terms (more): Switches, Toolkit, Foreman, Proteins, Antennae, Fruit fly, Mouse, Mice.
Hall of Amphibians: a hall with a frog and tadpole model. Key terms (more): Amphibian (Greek for double life), Amnion, Amniotes, Eardrum, Yolk sac, Jelly, Tadpole, Lily pad, Lizard, Scales. The first amniotes appeared more than 300 million years ago and soon split into a reptile and bird branch and a mammal branch.
Hall of Mammal Cousins: a long room of skulls of early relatives of mammals, who lived more than 200 million years ago. Articular and quadrate: the old reptile jaw hinge bones, which became the hammer and anvil in mammal ears; fossils with a double jaw hinge show the change. The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body, no bigger than a grain of rice. Key terms (more): Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup, Quadrate, Articular, Palaeontology, Whiskers, Milk.
Key terms (more): Goosebumps, Palmaris longus (missing in about one person in seven), Tendon, Coccyx, Tailbone, Platypus, Yolk, Fizzy, Womb, Unborn. Early in pregnancy a human embryo has a small tail that shrinks and leaves the tailbone. Humans carry a broken copy of a yolk gene; the platypus keeps a working copy. Hiccup ideas: a tadpole reflex, clearing air from a baby's stomach, exercising breathing muscles; none is proved.
Key terms (more): Appendix, Wisdom teeth, Haeckel, Hourglass, Upright, Compromises, Bench, Spine, Knees. Humans standing upright is a trade-off: the lower back, hips and knees take strain, but the hands are free. Some scientists think the appendix may shelter helpful gut bacteria; Dr Adjoa says to be careful with the word useless.
Tree Room: the last room, with a great painted tree of all backbone animals; a label says You are here. Trees built from fossils and trees built from DNA agree on nearly all of the main branches. At the end the hiccups stop on their own as the sun sets; Kofi's mother arrives at closing time. Key terms (more): Tree, Branches, Lobby, Streetlights.
chapters: The Egg That Left the Pond

beats.scene: Kofi hiccups loudly in front of a tall glass museum door
beats.summary: Kofi arrives at the museum with a bad case of hiccups.

beats.scene: Dr Adjoa waves from the museum steps holding a worn leather notebook
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa meets Kofi and says that even hiccups have a story.

beats.scene: A vast whale skeleton hangs from the roof of the main hall
beats.summary: Under a whale skeleton, Dr Adjoa says all animals with backbones share one plan.

beats.scene: Kofi reaches behind him and counts the bumps along his spine
beats.summary: Kofi feels his own backbone, a stack of small bones.

beats.scene: Visitors turn their heads as Kofi hiccups beside a glass case
beats.summary: Kofi has tried the usual hiccup cures, and none works, because no cure works for everyone.

beats.scene: Dr Adjoa draws a winding line across a museum map from hall to hall
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa plans the afternoon as a walk from the Fish Hall to the Hall of Mammals.

beats.scene: Dr Adjoa holds up her notebook open at a page of three rules
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa gives three rules for the day: ask what it is, ask how we know, and say when we are not sure.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dr Adjoa shake hands in front of a tall display case
beats.summary: Kofi bets that nobody can explain a hiccup, and Dr Adjoa promises to come back to it before closing.

beats.scene: A bright sign points to a staircase leading down to the oldest animals
beats.summary: A sign says the stairs lead down to the oldest animals, as the halls run from oldest to newest.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dr Adjoa walk down a stone staircase into blue light
beats.summary: Kofi follows Dr Adjoa down into the blue light of the old halls.

beats.scene: Kofi presses his nose against a cabinet of rocks, shells and bones
beats.summary: In the Hall of Clues, Dr Adjoa says scientists work like detectives, reading what was left behind.

beats.scene: A rock split open shows the shape of an ancient shell
beats.summary: The first clue is the fossil, the preserved remains or marks of an ancient living thing.

beats.scene: Two skeletons stand side by side with matching bones painted blue
beats.summary: The second clue is living bodies, which can be compared part by part.

beats.scene: A glowing model shows a tiny embryo curled in soft light
beats.summary: The third clue is the embryo, whose growth can reveal parts hidden in the adult.

beats.scene: A glowing double spiral of DNA floats above a glass case
beats.summary: The fourth clue is DNA, the instruction book inside cells, which is more alike in close relatives.

beats.scene: Rows of finches and beetles stand under bright lights on a long shelf
beats.summary: Kofi asks if anyone has seen evolution happen, and Dr Adjoa takes him to a shelf of finches and beetles.

beats.scene: Kofi studies beetles of different sizes and colours through a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Animals of one kind differ from each other, and some of the differences are inherited.

beats.scene: A finch with a deep beak cracks open a hard seed
beats.summary: Differences that help an animal to survive and have young become more common over time.

beats.scene: Finches with different beaks perch on a dry bush on a sunny island
beats.summary: Scientists measured finches on a Galápagos island during a drought and saw their beaks change.

beats.scene: A model of an old house shows rooms added over many years
beats.summary: Evolution has no goal or plan; it changes what already exists, so bodies are odd mixtures of old and new.

beats.scene: A rock split in two shows the outline of a small fish
beats.summary: In the Hall of Time, a split rock shows the stone outline of a small fish.

beats.scene: A fish skeleton sinks into soft mud on a quiet river floor
beats.summary: A fossil forms when a dead animal is buried quickly and its bones slowly turn to stone.

beats.scene: A huge cabinet holds a few small fossils among many empty trays
beats.summary: Very few animals become fossils, so the fossil record has gaps.

beats.scene: A cliff face shows flat layers of rock in many colours
beats.summary: Mud and sand settle in layers, and usually the deepest layer is the oldest.

beats.scene: Tilted and folded rock layers curve like a wave in a cliff
beats.summary: Layers can be tilted or folded, so scientists check each rock carefully.

beats.scene: The same spiral shell appears in rocks from two distant cliffs
beats.summary: The same kind of shell in distant rocks helps scientists match layers.

beats.scene: A glowing atom diagram stands beside an old ticking clock
beats.summary: Radioactive atoms change at a steady rate, and the time for half to change is called a half-life.

beats.scene: A grey layer of volcanic ash lies between two layers of rock
beats.summary: Volcanic ash layers can be dated, so a fossil between two of them has a known range of ages.

beats.scene: A glowing globe of Earth stands beside a huge number on a wall
beats.summary: The Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and the first animals with backbones came late.

beats.scene: A very long strip of cloth stretches the whole length of the hall
beats.summary: On a long strip of cloth, each step is a hundred million years, and people appear in the last sliver.

beats.scene: A glowing model of a Cambrian sea swarms with spiny, shelled animals
beats.summary: In the Fish Hall, a model of a Cambrian sea shows strange animals, almost none with a backbone.

beats.scene: Worms, snails, beetles and jellyfish are arranged in a colourful display
beats.summary: Most animals, then and now, have no backbone, so animals with backbones are one branch of many.

beats.scene: A diagram shows a stiff rod, a nerve cord and a tail
beats.summary: Animals with backbones belong to the chordates, which have four shared features at some stage of life.

beats.scene: A see-through lancelet lies half buried in sand inside a tank
beats.summary: The lancelet, a small sea animal with a stiff rod and no backbone, is a living clue.

beats.scene: Tiny fish-like fossils lie pressed into pale rock from China
beats.summary: Fossils from Chengjiang in China, about 520 million years old, may show some of the first vertebrates.

beats.scene: A model fish bends from side to side with its spine glowing
beats.summary: A backbone protects the nerve cord, anchors muscles and lets a body bend as it swims.

beats.scene: Kofi bends forward to touch his toes beside a giraffe skeleton
beats.summary: Kofi bends his spine and learns that he has seven neck bones, like a giraffe.

beats.scene: Kofi knocks softly on his forehead beside a skull in a case
beats.summary: The skull protects the brain, and in the first fish it was probably made of cartilage.

beats.scene: Stony helmets of armoured jawless fish stare out from a glass case
beats.summary: The first fish had no jaws, and some wore heavy plates of bone.

beats.scene: A lamprey clings to the glass of a tank by its round mouth
beats.summary: A living lamprey, a jawless fish, is a cousin and not an ancestor, but a good hint of early vertebrates.

beats.scene: A fish skeleton and a human skeleton stand side by side
beats.summary: A fish and a person share one basic plan of skull, spine and ribs.

beats.scene: A diagram shows curved bars supporting the gills along a fish's head
beats.summary: In fish, curved bars called gill arches hold up the gills.

beats.scene: A cutaway diagram of one gill arch shows bone, muscle, nerve and vessel
beats.summary: Each gill arch is a kit of parts: a bar, a muscle, a nerve and a blood vessel.

beats.scene: A street of identical houses, with one that has a big new kitchen
beats.summary: Repeated parts let one copy change while the others keep doing the old job.

beats.scene: A model shows a front gill arch growing larger and hinging into a jaw
beats.summary: In some early fish, the front gill arches grew larger and hinged to become jaws.

beats.scene: A fish with jaws bites a hard shell beside a jawless fish
beats.summary: Jaws let fish bite and crush many new foods, and jawed fish spread widely.

beats.scene: A cast of a huge armoured fish skull hangs above a doorway
beats.summary: Dunkleosteus, an armoured fish of about 370 million years ago, shows what a gill arch can become.

beats.scene: Kofi opens his mouth with one finger resting in front of his ear
beats.summary: Kofi feels his jaw hinge move just in front of his ear.

beats.scene: A diagram of embryo neck folds is coloured to show jaw, ear and throat
beats.summary: In a human embryo, the first arch builds the jaw, and later arches build ear bones and parts of the throat.

beats.scene: Kofi yawns widely beside a model of a shark's small breathing hole
beats.summary: A tube from the ear to the throat belongs to the same family of parts as a shark's spiracle.

beats.scene: A shark's open jaw shows rows of teeth beside a patch of rough skin
beats.summary: Beside a shark's jaw, Kofi touches a patch of shark skin that feels like sandpaper.

beats.scene: A microscope view shows tiny pointed scales covering a shark's skin
beats.summary: Shark skin is covered in denticles, tiny scales built like teeth.

beats.scene: A diagram shows skin scales spreading into a fish's mouth and growing into teeth
beats.summary: Scientists think teeth began as skin scales that spread into the mouth.

beats.scene: Rows of shark teeth move forward like a slow conveyor belt
beats.summary: A shark keeps replacing its teeth from rows behind, and may use thousands in a lifetime.

beats.scene: Kofi pulls back his lip to show a gap in his teeth
beats.summary: Kofi has lost a baby tooth, and people get only two sets of teeth.

beats.scene: A cutaway tooth shows a glassy white coat over bone-like material
beats.summary: Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the body, and it does not grow back.

beats.scene: A pale grey shark skeleton hangs beside a stiff white fish bone
beats.summary: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, which is light and bendy, not of bone.

beats.scene: Kofi bends the rim of his ear and presses the tip of his nose
beats.summary: Kofi's ears and nose are made of cartilage, the same material as a shark's skeleton.

beats.scene: A diagram of a baby's skeleton shows grey cartilage turning white as bone
beats.summary: Much of a baby's skeleton starts as cartilage, which is replaced by bone as the child grows.

beats.scene: A family tree splits into sharks on one branch and bony fish on another
beats.summary: Jawed fish split into sharks with cartilage and bony fish, and humans belong to the bony side.

beats.scene: A glowing model of a human embryo shows small folds on its neck
beats.summary: In the Hall of Beginnings, a model of an embryo shows small folds on the neck, called arches.

beats.scene: A diagram shows an embryo's neck folds with arrows to jaw, ear and throat
beats.summary: The folds are not gills: they never breathe, and they become the jaw, ear and throat.

beats.scene: Kofi stares in alarm at his own neck in a small round mirror
beats.summary: Kofi asks whether he once had gills, and Dr Adjoa says he had a fish's starting parts, not its gills.

beats.scene: Pieces of a baby's face grow towards each other and meet in the middle
beats.summary: A face is built from separate pieces of tissue that grow together and join.

beats.scene: A glowing tube heart folds into a curve inside a tiny embryo
beats.summary: The human heart begins as a simple tube that starts to pulse in the first weeks.

beats.scene: A series of models shows a heart tube looping and dividing
beats.summary: The heart tube loops and grows walls that divide it into chambers.

beats.scene: Three glass heart models stand in a row with two, three and four chambers
beats.summary: Fish hearts have two chambers, amphibians three and mammals four.

beats.scene: A heart diagram shows red and blue blood kept apart in four chambers
beats.summary: Four chambers keep blood rich in oxygen apart from used blood, which suits warm-blooded animals.

beats.scene: Blood vessels run through a fish's gill arches beside matching vessels in an embryo
beats.summary: Blood vessels that run through a fish's gill arches are rebuilt in the embryo as the great vessels of the neck and heart.

beats.scene: A recipe book lies open beside a glowing model of an embryo
beats.summary: An embryo does not pass through a fish stage; it follows an old growth recipe that changes a little at a time.

beats.scene: A fish head diagram shows bright nerve lines running to each gill arch
beats.summary: Nerves in our head and neck follow paths first laid down in fish.

beats.scene: Coloured nerve lines run from a human brain to jaw, face and throat
beats.summary: Each arch has its own nerve in a fish, and the same lineup serves our jaw, face and throat.

beats.scene: Kofi pulls faces at his own reflection in a glass case
beats.summary: The muscles that make facial expressions come from the second arch, which works the gill cover in fish.

beats.scene: A long nerve winds from the brain to the neck, heart and gut
beats.summary: The vagus nerve, whose name means wandering, runs from the brain to the neck, heart and gut.

beats.scene: A diagram beside a giraffe skeleton shows a nerve looping under a blood vessel
beats.summary: A nerve to the voice box loops down and back up the neck, a long detour in a giraffe.

beats.scene: A fish diagram shows a short straight nerve passing beside a blood vessel
beats.summary: In fish the nerve ran straight past a blood vessel, and it stayed hooked there as necks grew longer.

beats.scene: A long neck model shows a stretched nerve looping around a blood vessel
beats.summary: Evolution cannot start again, so a body keeps old routes even when they are not the best design.

beats.scene: A human neck diagram shows a short nerve loop under the great artery
beats.summary: People have the same nerve loop, much shorter than in a giraffe.

beats.scene: A diaphragm drops from the neck to the chest, its nerve trailing behind
beats.summary: The diaphragm's nerve starts in the neck because the muscle begins near the neck in the embryo and moves down.

beats.scene: A passing guard jumps as Kofi hiccups beside a nerve diagram
beats.summary: Each hic is a jerk of the diaphragm followed by a snap shut of the voice box, along old nerve pathways.

beats.scene: A glowing diagram shows a pair of lungs inside an ancient fish
beats.summary: Lungs first appeared in early bony fish, long before any animal walked on land.

beats.scene: A fish hovers in mid-water with a glowing gas bag inside its body
beats.summary: The swim bladder of many fish, a gas bag for floating, probably descends from early lungs.

beats.scene: A bichir rises to the surface of a tank to gulp air
beats.summary: The bichir, a living fish, has gills and simple lungs and gulps air at the surface.

beats.scene: A lungfish curls in a mud burrow as its river dries up
beats.summary: A lungfish breathes air through lungs and can survive for months in dried mud.

beats.scene: Crowded fish gasp at the surface of a warm, shallow pool
beats.summary: Warm shallow water holds little oxygen, while air holds plenty, so gulping air could save a fish.

beats.scene: A small bud grows from a throat tube and branches like a tree
beats.summary: In an embryo, the lungs begin as a bud that grows out of the throat tube and branches.

beats.scene: A diagram shows food and air paths crossing, with a small flap closing
beats.summary: Because the lungs grew from the throat, air and food share a passage, and food sometimes goes the wrong way.

beats.scene: Branching lung tubes end in tiny glowing air sacs wrapped in blood vessels
beats.summary: Human lungs hold hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs with a huge surface for oxygen.

beats.scene: The voice box flap snaps shut like a small door above the windpipe
beats.summary: The voice box can snap shut to keep water and food out of the lungs, a useful guard for air breathers.

beats.scene: Kofi takes a deep breath while Dr Adjoa counts on her fingers
beats.summary: Kofi holds a deep breath and his hiccups pause for a moment before returning.

beats.scene: A fish's side shows a faint line of tiny pores along its body
beats.summary: Fish sense water movement with a lateral line along each side.

beats.scene: Tiny hairs on a glowing hair cell bend as water ripples past
beats.summary: The lateral line holds hair cells whose tiny hairs bend with the water and send signals along nerves.

beats.scene: A school of silver fish turns together beside a shark in dim water
beats.summary: Fish in schools and hunting sharks both use the lateral line.

beats.scene: Glowing hair cells inside a model of a human ear
beats.summary: The hair cells of our inner ear are the same kind, and fish can regrow them while mammals mostly cannot.

beats.scene: Three fluid-filled loops sit at right angles inside a model ear
beats.summary: Our three balance loops are very like a fish's.

beats.scene: Kofi spins on the spot with his arms out in the museum hall
beats.summary: Kofi spins and feels dizzy because the fluid in his ear loops keeps moving.

beats.scene: A tiny ear stone with growth rings sits beside a fish skull
beats.summary: Fish have ear stones called otoliths that grow in rings, and humans have tiny balance crystals.

beats.scene: Cutaway diagrams of a fish eye, a human eye and an octopus eye
beats.summary: Fish and human eyes share a camera plan, with a blind spot, while the octopus eye evolved separately.

beats.scene: A rainbow of coloured light falls on a goldfish eye in clear water
beats.summary: Ancient fish saw four colours, most mammals lost two, and primates regained a third.

beats.scene: A wall of small glass bottles holds different smells while Kofi sniffs one
beats.summary: Humans have about 400 working smell genes and many broken ones, a sign of keener noses in some ancestors.

beats.scene: Drawings of a fish fin and a human arm with matching coloured bones
beats.summary: A lobe fin and a human arm contain bones in the same pattern: one, two, then many.

beats.scene: A paper fan beside a fleshy lobed fin with bones inside
beats.summary: Most fish have ray fins, but lobe-finned fish have fleshy fins with bones, and they are on our side of the family tree.

beats.scene: A model of a coelacanth hangs in a corner of the hall
beats.summary: The coelacanth, a lobe-finned fish thought extinct, was found alive in 1938.

beats.scene: Kofi squeezes his upper arm beside a glowing humerus bone
beats.summary: The single bone of the upper arm, the humerus, matches the single large bone of the fin.

beats.scene: Kofi turns his palm up and down beside a forearm skeleton
beats.summary: The two forearm bones, radius and ulna, match the two bones in the fin and cross as the palm turns.

beats.scene: A skeleton hand with wrist bones and finger bones glows on a table
beats.summary: The wrist and finger bones match the spread of many small bones in the fin.

beats.scene: A bat wing, whale flipper, horse leg and mole paw show matching bones
beats.summary: The same bone pattern appears in the bat's wing, the whale's flipper and the horse's leg.

beats.scene: A tiny limb bud grows a flat paddle that is carved into fingers
beats.summary: In an embryo, the hand starts as a paddle, and fingers appear when cells between them die away.

beats.scene: A zebrafish fin and a mouse paw glow with the same gene colours
beats.summary: Some genes that shape fish fins also help to shape hands, so the same toolkit was reused.

beats.scene: Kofi wriggles his fingers in blue light beside an old fin fossil
beats.summary: A fin became a hand through many small steps, each useful or harmless, with no plan.

beats.scene: A long case shows a Devonian river bank with strange green plants
beats.summary: In the Hall of Shores, a model shows a Devonian river bank about 400 million years ago, the Age of Fishes.

beats.scene: Mosses, low plants and tiny insects cover a muddy river shore
beats.summary: Plants and small animals such as insects had reached the land before animals with backbones.

beats.scene: A giant sea scorpion lurks in a warm, crowded, shallow pool
beats.summary: The warm shallow water was crowded and short of oxygen, with large hunters such as giant sea scorpions.

beats.scene: Sunlit mud banks hold insects and few hunters beside a pool
beats.summary: The shore offered food and perhaps fewer enemies, so a fish that could briefly leave the water might do well.

beats.scene: A fish with strong fins props itself up in a shallow pool
beats.summary: Lungs to gulp air and strong fins to prop up the body were already present in some fish.

beats.scene: A mudskipper props itself on strong front fins on tidal mud
beats.summary: Mudskippers, which are not our relatives, show that a fish can manage on land for a while.

beats.scene: Kofi looks puzzled in front of a pool where fish crowd together
beats.summary: A fish does not plan to leave the water; animals that cope well simply leave more young.

beats.scene: A river floods its banks while a nearby pool cracks dry in the sun
beats.summary: In some regions rivers flooded and dried, and many fossils come from rocks that were once rivers.

beats.scene: A long strip of fossils shows fish slowly changing into four-legged animals
beats.summary: The change from fleshy-finned fish to legged animals took many millions of years.

beats.scene: A heavy wooden door has gold letters reading Gallery of In-Betweens
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa opens the door to the Gallery of In-Betweens, where the star of the afternoon waits.

beats.scene: A cast of Tiktaalik stands under bright spotlights in a dark room
beats.summary: In the Gallery of In-Betweens stands a cast of Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, found in Arctic Canada.

beats.scene: A sign beside the cast shows the name Tiktaalik and an Arctic map
beats.summary: The name Tiktaalik comes from Inuktitut and means a large freshwater fish.

beats.scene: Tiktaalik lies in shallow water with its flat head and eyes above the surface
beats.summary: Tiktaalik had scales, fins and gills like a fish, but a flat head with eyes on top like a crocodile's.

beats.scene: Tiktaalik turns its flat head while its body rests in the shallows
beats.summary: Unlike most fish, Tiktaalik could move its head separately from its body: it had a neck.

beats.scene: An animal's head turns to snap at an insect while its body stays still
beats.summary: A neck lets the head look and strike while the body stays still, and it is useful on land.

beats.scene: Tiktaalik props its chest up on strong fins at the edge of a pool
beats.summary: Tiktaalik's front fins had a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist-like joint, so it could push up.

beats.scene: A glowing diagram shows the broad, overlapping ribs of Tiktaalik
beats.summary: Tiktaalik's strong ribs could help to hold up its body when it was out of the water.

beats.scene: Tiktaalik gulps air at the surface through openings on its head
beats.summary: Tiktaalik had gills and probably lungs, and its head openings may have helped it to gulp air.

beats.scene: Fossils of a flat fish, Tiktaalik and a legged animal stand in a row
beats.summary: Tiktaalik mixes fish and early four-legged features, and is probably a close cousin of our ancestors.

beats.scene: Kofi swings his whole body to look at a painting on the wall
beats.summary: Kofi tries looking around without turning his neck and decides that Tiktaalik had a good idea.

beats.scene: A cast of Acanthostega with eight fingers on each front foot
beats.summary: Acanthostega, from Greenland about 365 million years ago, had limbs with fingers but also gills.

beats.scene: A cast of Ichthyostega rests on a model mudbank
beats.summary: Ichthyostega, another early four-legged animal from Greenland, had seven toes on each back foot.

beats.scene: Six, seven and eight-fingered limbs are drawn above a five-fingered hand
beats.summary: Many early tetrapods had more than five fingers, and five became the usual number later.

beats.scene: Acanthostega paddles underwater with its limbs among weeds
beats.summary: Acanthostega's limbs were too weak for land, so legs probably first served in water.

beats.scene: Four-limbed footprints are pressed into an old stone shoreline
beats.summary: In 2010, scientists reported four-limbed tracks from Poland, nearly 400 million years old and older than Tiktaalik.

beats.scene: A branching bush of animals is drawn on a wall instead of a ladder
beats.summary: The tracks show that the family tree is more like a bush than a ladder.

beats.scene: Kofi places his hand beside a cast of ancient footprints
beats.summary: Kofi touches a cast of the Polish tracks and feels that something with toes walked there long ago.

beats.scene: A pelvis bone joins firmly to a backbone beside a leg bone
beats.summary: Land animals need strong hips firmly joined to the backbone to carry their weight.

beats.scene: A frog, a snake, a bird and a whale hang from one branching tree
beats.summary: Tetrapod means four feet, and the group includes every descendant of the first ones, even snakes and whales.

beats.scene: Kofi looks at a fish skeleton and then at his own hand
beats.summary: On the family tree Kofi is a kind of bony fish, just as a sparrow is a kind of dinosaur.

beats.scene: Glowing screens show a long DNA strand split into short recipe cards
beats.summary: In the Gene Gallery, a gene is explained as a short stretch of DNA that works like a recipe.

beats.scene: A fly and a person stand beside matching coloured bands along their bodies
beats.summary: Hox genes lay out the body from head to tail in flies, fish and people.

beats.scene: A fruit fly with legs growing from its head sits in a lab dish
beats.summary: A small change in a Hox gene can make a fruit fly grow legs where its antennae should be.

beats.scene: A conductor stands before an orchestra of glowing gene icons
beats.summary: Switches in the DNA decide when and where genes are used, and many evolutionary changes are in the switches.

beats.scene: A small striped zebrafish swims in a lab tank under a magnifying lens
beats.summary: About seven in ten human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish, which scientists use to study the body.

beats.scene: A see-through zebrafish embryo shows a beating heart under a microscope
beats.summary: Zebrafish embryos are transparent, so scientists can watch the body build itself and test what each gene does.

beats.scene: A fly's eye and a human eye share the same glowing gene
beats.summary: A gene called Pax6 helps to build eyes in flies, fish and people.

beats.scene: A glowing toolbox of gene tools sits beside a fly, fish and boy
beats.summary: Animals share a toolkit of old genes and use it differently to build different bodies.

beats.scene: Researchers peer at tiny flies, fish and mice in a bright laboratory
beats.summary: Shared genes mean that studies of fish, flies and mice can help us to understand human bodies.

beats.scene: A clock with DNA hands sits beside a dated fossil
beats.summary: DNA changes slowly at a fairly steady pace, so differences between animals can work as a rough clock that scientists check against fossils.

beats.scene: A frog sits on a lily pad while a tadpole wriggles below
beats.summary: In the Hall of Amphibians, a frog and a tadpole show a double life in water and on land.

beats.scene: A tadpole with gills and a tail swims beside a frog with legs
beats.summary: A tadpole breathes with gills and swims with a tail, then grows lungs and legs to become a frog.

beats.scene: A frog's moist skin shines in the mist beside a pond
beats.summary: Frogs breathe partly through moist skin, so most amphibians must live near water.

beats.scene: A clump of jelly-covered frog eggs floats in a pond
beats.summary: Frog eggs are soft jelly with no shell, so they must be laid in water.

beats.scene: A frog model shows a round disc of skin behind the eye
beats.summary: A frog's eardrum picks up sound from the air, a problem that fish did not have to solve.

beats.scene: A tough-shelled egg cracks open to show a baby reptile inside
beats.summary: Reptiles evolved eggs with shells and membranes that can be laid on dry land.

beats.scene: A fluid-filled bag surrounds a tiny human embryo like a small pond
beats.summary: One egg membrane, the amnion, is a bag of fluid, and a human baby grows inside one too.

beats.scene: A yolk sac hangs beside a bird embryo and a human embryo
beats.summary: A human embryo has a small yolk sac without real yolk, which makes early blood cells.

beats.scene: A lizard with dry scaly skin basks on a dry rock
beats.summary: Dry scaly skin and better lungs let reptiles live far from water.

beats.scene: A tree splits into a reptile and bird branch and a mammal branch
beats.summary: The amniotes split into a reptile and bird branch and a mammal branch more than 300 million years ago.

beats.scene: A long hall of skulls with sharp teeth lit by small lamps
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa and Kofi enter the Hall of Mammal Cousins, full of skulls of early relatives of mammals.

beats.scene: A skull's lower jaw shows several bones joined by seams
beats.summary: Early mammal relatives had a lower jaw made of several bones, while a mammal's is a single bone.

beats.scene: A diagram shows a reptile jaw hinge made from two small bones
beats.summary: In a reptile, the jaw hinge is made by the articular and quadrate bones, but in a mammal by other bones.

beats.scene: A fossil jaw has two hinges side by side, one old and one new
beats.summary: A few fossils of mammal cousins have two jaw hinges at once, showing how the change happened safely.

beats.scene: Three tiny ear bones named hammer, anvil and stirrup are drawn large
beats.summary: Mammals have three ear bones, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, which carry sound from the eardrum to the inner ear.

beats.scene: Arrows show two jaw hinge bones moving into the middle ear
beats.summary: The hammer and anvil are the old reptile jaw hinge bones, which shrank and moved into the ear.

beats.scene: A small light ear bone vibrates beside a drawn sound wave
beats.summary: Small light ear bones pass on high sounds well, and the new jaw hinge may have made the bite stronger.

beats.scene: An embryo diagram shows two jaw bones separating and moving to the ear
beats.summary: In a human embryo, the hammer and anvil form near the jaw and then move to the middle ear.

beats.scene: Kofi touches his ear while a stirrup bone glows beside a grain of rice
beats.summary: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body, no bigger than a grain of rice.

beats.scene: A furry mammal feeds its young in a nest in a quiet diorama
beats.summary: Only mammals have hair and make milk, features that began in their early ancestors.

beats.scene: Kofi's arm with raised hairs and goosebumps in the cool museum air
beats.summary: In the cool museum air Kofi gets goosebumps, a reflex older than humans.

beats.scene: A close-up of a hair standing up as a tiny muscle pulls it
beats.summary: A tiny muscle pulls each hair upright, which in furry animals fluffs the fur to keep warm or look big.

beats.scene: Kofi grimaces as he tries to wiggle his ears
beats.summary: Some people can wiggle their ears, using small muscles left over from ancestors that turned their ears towards sounds.

beats.scene: Kofi presses thumb to little finger and a thin cord stands on his wrist
beats.summary: A wrist tendon, the palmaris longus, is missing in about one person in seven with almost no effect.

beats.scene: A human embryo with a curved tail sits beside a drawing of the tailbone
beats.summary: Early in pregnancy a human embryo has a small tail, which shrinks and leaves the tailbone.

beats.scene: A broken yolk gene is drawn as a torn page in a recipe book
beats.summary: People carry a broken copy of a gene that makes yolk, a trace of egg-laying ancestors.

beats.scene: A torn recipe page lies beside a row of broken smell genes
beats.summary: A gene that is no longer needed can break without harm, so DNA holds many remains such as broken smell genes.

beats.scene: A tadpole breathes with feathery gills while a frog swallows air nearby
beats.summary: One idea says hiccups come from a reflex used by tadpoles, but scientists are not sure.

beats.scene: An unborn baby hiccups on a soft ultrasound screen
beats.summary: Unborn babies hiccup long before they breathe air, so other ideas about hiccups exist too.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dr Adjoa stand before a wall sign with a large question mark
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa says that no one yet knows why we hiccup, though the hiccup is a nerve reflex.

beats.scene: Kofi sits on a bench and rubs his lower back
beats.summary: Kofi sits down with a tired back, and Dr Adjoa says that walking upright has a price.

beats.scene: A four-legged skeleton's spine like a bridge stands beside an upright human spine
beats.summary: In four-legged mammals the spine is like a bridge, but in people it stands on end, and the lower back carries a heavy load.

beats.scene: A human skeleton shows hip, knee and foot bones carrying the body's weight
beats.summary: Walking on two legs puts strain on hips and knees but frees the hands.

beats.scene: A jaw model shows too little room for the last teeth
beats.summary: Many people lack room for wisdom teeth, probably because human jaws became shorter over time.

beats.scene: A small pouch on a model gut glows beside a question mark
beats.summary: The appendix was once called useless, but some scientists think it may help the gut, so science keeps testing ideas.

beats.scene: An old drawing of embryos sits beside a modern scan of real ones
beats.summary: Old drawings of embryos exaggerated the likeness, but the real similarities are still true.

beats.scene: An hourglass shape runs through a row of embryo drawings of many animals
beats.summary: Careful studies suggest that backbone animals look most alike at a middle stage, but scientists still debate it.

beats.scene: A ladder is crossed out and a branching tree is drawn beside it
beats.summary: No living animal is higher or lower; all have evolved for the same time and fit their own way of life.

beats.scene: A balance scale weighs strength against speed on a wall chart
beats.summary: Every body is a bundle of compromises that works well enough, and the leftovers are evidence of history.

beats.scene: Golden light falls through tall windows on a quiet, nearly empty hall
beats.summary: The windows turn gold as the afternoon ends, and Dr Adjoa says there is one room left.

beats.scene: A huge painted tree of backbone animals covers a long museum wall
beats.summary: In the Tree Room, all backbone animals fit on one family tree.

beats.scene: Two matching family trees, one built from bones and one from DNA
beats.summary: Trees built from fossils and trees built from DNA agree on most of the main branches.

beats.scene: A small label reading You are here sits at the end of a branch
beats.summary: Kofi finds himself on the tree and traces his line back through a mouse, lizard, frog, lungfish, shark and lamprey.

beats.scene: A scientist brushes dust from a fossil bone in a bright field camp
beats.summary: New fossils keep being found, and science keeps testing and improving the story.

beats.scene: A scientist checks a fossil against a chart of rock layers
beats.summary: A good idea in science must be open to being proved wrong, and the evolution story has passed its tests so far.

beats.scene: Kofi reads three rules aloud from Dr Adjoa's worn notebook
beats.summary: Kofi recites the three rules from memory: ask what it is, ask how we know, and say when we are not sure.

beats.scene: Kofi opens his hand wide and studies his fingers in golden light
beats.summary: Kofi looks at his hand and thinks of the fins, bones and fish that came before.

beats.scene: Dr Adjoa and Kofi talk quietly in the nearly empty gallery
beats.summary: Dr Adjoa keeps her promise: a hiccup is a nerve reflex of the diaphragm and voice box, but its original reason is unknown.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dr Adjoa stand at the glass doors as the sun sets
beats.summary: Kofi's hiccups finally stop, quietly, as the sun sets.

beats.scene: Kofi runs down the museum steps to meet his mother at sunset
beats.summary: Kofi leaves with his mother, understanding that his body is a living museum.

Kofi bets that nobody can truly explain a hiccup. Dr Adjoa laughs and promises to return to his hiccups before closing time, although she warns that some parts are still a mystery.
At the end of the hall, a sign says that the stairs lead down to the oldest animals in the museum. Dr Adjoa grins and says that in this building, the deeper you go, the older it gets.
Kofi follows her down the stone stairs, and each hiccup echoes against the walls. It feels as if he is walking into a very old and very quiet world.
In the Hall of Clues, Kofi presses his nose against a cabinet of rocks, bones, shells and one old microscope. Dr Adjoa says that these are the tools for reading the past.
The first kind of clue is the fossil, the remains or the marks of a living thing preserved in rock. Fossils show what bodies looked like long before anyone was there to see them.

The second kind of clue is the body of a living animal, which can be compared piece by piece. When two animals share an unusual part that is built in the same way, scientists suspect that they share an ancestor.
The third kind of clue is the embryo, the earliest stage of a growing body. Watching how a body builds itself can reveal parts that are hidden in the finished animal.
The fourth kind of clue is DNA, the long set of instructions inside the cells of every living thing. Parents pass it to their young, and close relatives have DNA that is more alike.
Kofi asks whether anybody has ever watched evolution happen. Dr Adjoa leads him to a shelf where finches and beetles of many kinds stand under bright lights.
Look closely at the beetles, says Dr Adjoa, and you will see that no two are exactly alike. Some of those differences pass from parents to young, and that is where evolution begins.
Some differences help an animal to find food or to escape from danger. Animals with a helpful difference tend to leave more young, so that difference becomes more common.

On a small island in the Galápagos, scientists measured finches during a long drought. The birds with larger beaks could crack the hard seeds, so more of them survived, and their young had bigger beaks on average.
Dr Adjoa warns that evolution has no goal and no plan. It can only change the parts that already exist, so bodies are often odd mixtures of old and new.
In the Hall of Time, Dr Adjoa lifts a rock that has been split in half. On its face lies the stone outline of a small fish that died long before there were people.
When a fish dies and sinks into soft mud, its body may be buried before anything eats it. Over a very long time, minerals fill its bones and the mud hardens into rock.
Very few animals ever become fossils, because most are eaten or rot away completely. That means the fossil record has many gaps, and every new find is a lucky survivor.
Over time, mud and sand settle in layers, each one on top of the last. Usually the oldest layer is at the bottom, so deeper rock is normally older, like the first page in a pile.
Sometimes the movements of the Earth tilt, fold or break the layers. Scientists therefore check each rock with care, because the rule that the oldest is at the bottom is usually true but not always.
Some kinds of shell lived for a limited time and spread over a wide area. When the same shell turns up in rocks far apart, scientists can match the layers and compare their ages.
Radioactive atoms change into other atoms at a steady, known speed. The time it takes for half of them to change is called a half-life, and it can be measured very precisely.
Volcanic ash falls in layers and can be dated with radioactive atoms. A fossil found between two ash layers must be younger than the lower one and older than the upper one.

The Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and scientists think that life began at least three billion years ago. Animals with backbones came along much later, only in the last part of the story.

Dr Adjoa unrolls a long strip of cloth and says that each step along it stands for a hundred million years. The whole story of backbones fits into the last few steps, and people appear at the very end.
The first case in the Fish Hall holds a model of a Cambrian sea, from more than five hundred million years ago. It swarms with strange animals, and almost none of them has a backbone.
Even today, most animals have no backbone at all. Worms, snails, insects, spiders and jellyfish all manage perfectly well without one.
Animals with backbones belong to a larger group called the chordates. As embryos, chordates have a stiff rod along the back, a nerve cord above it, a tail and slits in the throat.
In a sandy tank lives a lancelet, a small see-through animal that looks like a thin fish. It has a stiff rod and a nerve cord but no backbone, which makes it a useful clue.

In the rocks of Chengjiang in China, scientists have found fossils about five hundred and twenty million years old. A few tiny animals among them look like early fish, although scientists still discuss exactly where they belong.
A backbone protects the nerve cord and gives the muscles something firm to pull on. It lets a body bend from side to side, which is how a fish swims.
Kofi bends forward to touch his toes and feels his back curve. Dr Adjoa tells him that he has seven bones in his neck, and so does a giraffe.
At the front end of the backbone sits the skull, a strong case that protects the brain. Kofi knocks gently on his forehead and feels the hard bone beneath the skin.
The first fish had no jaws at all, only a round mouth that sucked or filtered food. Some of them wore heavy plates of bone, like tiny knights.
In a tank clings a lamprey, a living fish with a round mouth full of teeth and no jaws. Dr Adjoa says it is not our ancestor, but a cousin that helps us to imagine early vertebrates.
In the next room, a fish skeleton and a human skeleton stand side by side. Both have a skull, a spine and ribs, even though one swims and the other walks.
Fish breathe with gills, which take oxygen from the water. Curved bars of bone or soft cartilage, called gill arches, hold the gills in place on each side of the head.
Each gill arch is really a small kit of useful parts, built to a standard pattern. It has a bar of bone or cartilage, a muscle, a nerve and a blood vessel.
Imagine a street of identical houses, says Dr Adjoa, where one family builds a grand new kitchen. The other houses still work as before, so nothing is lost.
Scientists think that in some early fish the front gill arches grew larger and developed a hinge. Over a very long time, they became jaws that could open wide and snap shut.
Jaws let a fish grab, bite and crush its food instead of just sucking it up. Fish with jaws could eat many more kinds of food, and they soon spread through the seas.

A skull cast in the hall belongs to Dunkleosteus, an armoured fish that lived about three hundred and seventy million years ago. Its jaws had sharp edges of bone instead of teeth, and they could probably cut through the armour of other fish.
Kofi opens and closes his mouth and puts a finger just in front of his ear. He can feel the hinge of his own jaw sliding beneath the skin.
In a human embryo, the first arch builds much of the jaw, and it also helps to shape the face. Later arches build small bones of the ear and many parts of the throat and neck.
Kofi yawns so widely that his ears pop, and the hall suddenly sounds clearer. Dr Adjoa says that the tube joining the ear to the throat belongs to the same family as a shark's small breathing hole.
In the next case, the jaw of a shark opens wide, showing row behind row of sharp teeth. Beside it lies a patch of shark skin that feels as rough as sandpaper.
Shark skin is covered with denticles, which are tiny pointed scales. Under a microscope, each has a hard coat, a bony core and a soft centre with nerves and blood vessels.
Scientists think that teeth began as tough scales in the skin. Over time, some of those scales moved into the mouth and became teeth that could bite.
A shark's teeth sit in several rows, and new ones keep moving forward to replace broken ones. Over its life, a single shark may use thousands of teeth.
Kofi shows Dr Adjoa a gap where a baby tooth fell out last week. People get only two sets of teeth, unlike a shark, so the second set has to last.
The outer layer of a tooth, called enamel, is the hardest material in the human body. It cannot grow back once it is worn away, which is why teeth need care.
In a nearby case hangs a shark skeleton, grey and rubbery. It is made of cartilage, a firm but bendy material that is lighter than bone.
Kofi bends the top of his ear and the tip of his nose. They are made of cartilage, the same kind of material as a shark's skeleton.
A newborn baby has many more soft cartilage parts than an adult does. During childhood, much of the cartilage is slowly replaced by bone, and many small bones join together.
Jawed fish split long ago into two great groups. Sharks and rays have skeletons of cartilage, while the bony fish, our own branch, have skeletons of bone.
In the Hall of Beginnings, a glowing model shows a human embryo only a few weeks old. On its neck are small folds, called arches, that look like the ridges of a tiny accordion.
The embryo never breathes with these folds, because it gets its oxygen from its mother's blood. Instead, the folds grow into the jaw, the ear and the throat.
Kofi asks, with some alarm, whether he once had gills. Dr Adjoa laughs and says that he had the same starting parts as a fish, but not a fish's gills.
A baby's face is built from several separate pieces of tissue that grow towards each other. They meet and join in the middle, like the two sides of a zip.
The heart is one of the first organs to work. It begins as a simple tube that starts to pulse when the embryo is only a few weeks old.
Over the next weeks, the heart tube bends and loops back on itself. Walls grow inside it and divide it into four separate chambers.
Three glass models of hearts stand side by side along the wall of the hall. A fish heart has two chambers, a frog heart has three, and a mammal heart has four.
A four-chambered heart keeps blood that is full of oxygen apart from blood that has used it up. That helps warm-blooded animals such as mammals, which need a lot of energy.
In a fish, big blood vessels run through each gill arch to carry blood to the gills. In a human embryo, the same kind of vessels form, and then they are rebuilt into the great vessels near the heart.
An embryo does not turn into a fish and then into a person. Instead, it follows a growth recipe that has been changed a little at a time, and the oldest steps are often kept.
On the wall is a diagram of a fish's head with a nerve running into each gill arch. Dr Adjoa says that people have twelve pairs of nerves in the head, and many of them follow the same old paths.
In a fish, a different nerve serves each of the gill arches, from the front to the back. In us, one nerve still serves the jaw muscles and the skin of the face, and another serves the throat.
Kofi smiles, frowns and raises one eyebrow at his reflection in a glass case. The muscles that move his face come from the second arch, which in fish helps to work the gill cover.
One nerve in the head has a very long journey. It is called the vagus, which means wandering, and it runs from the brain down through the neck to the heart and the gut.
A nerve to the voice box goes down the neck, loops under a blood vessel near the heart and climbs back up. In a giraffe, with its great neck, that detour is very long indeed.
In a fish, this nerve ran straight to the last gill arch, passing close to a blood vessel. As necks grew longer and hearts moved down, the nerve stayed hooked around the vessel and was stretched.
Evolution can only change what already exists, and it never goes back to start again. A designer would have chosen a straight path, but a changing body keeps its old routes.
People have the same loop, though it is much shorter than a giraffe's. The nerve on the left side hooks under the great artery from the heart before climbing up to the voice box.
The diaphragm is the sheet of muscle under your lungs. Its nerve starts high in the neck, because in the embryo the diaphragm begins up near the neck and then moves down.

At that very moment Kofi hiccups again, loudly enough to make a passing guard jump. Dr Adjoa explains that each hic is a sudden jerk of the diaphragm, followed at once by a snap shut of the voice box.
A diagram shows a pair of lungs inside the body of an ancient fish. Scientists think that lungs first appeared in early bony fish, long before any animal walked on land.
Most bony fish today have a swim bladder, a bag of gas that helps them to float. Many scientists think that it is a descendant of the old lungs.
In the next tank swims a bichir, an African fish that has gills and a pair of simple lungs. It rises to the surface now and then to gulp a mouthful of air.
African lungfish live in rivers that sometimes dry up, and they can breathe air through true lungs. Some can survive for months in dried mud, breathing air the whole time.
Warm, shallow water often holds very little oxygen, while air is full of it. A fish that could gulp air could survive in pools where other fish struggled.
In an embryo, the lungs begin as a small bud that grows out from the throat. The bud divides again and again, like a tree putting out branches.

Because the lungs grew out of the throat, air and food share one passage for a short way. A flap called the epiglottis usually covers the windpipe when we swallow, but food sometimes slips the wrong way.
Branching tubes in the lungs end in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs. Spread out flat, their thin walls would cover an area much larger than Kofi's bedroom floor.
The voice box can close like a door to keep water and food out of the lungs. Any animal that breathes air near water needs a good door.
Kofi takes a long, deep breath and holds it. The hiccups stop for a few seconds, but then they come back as loud as ever.
A fish has a faint line along each side of its body. This lateral line lets it sense the movement of the water around it, even in the dark.
Under the pores are hair cells, each with a bundle of tiny hairs on top. When the water moves, the hairs bend, and the cell sends a signal along a nerve.
A school of fish can turn all at once, partly because each fish feels the movement of its neighbours. Sharks also use the same sense to find injured prey in the dark.
Deep inside your ear are hair cells of the same kind. They detect the tiny shakes of sound, and they also help you to keep your balance.
Above the hearing part of the ear sit three tiny loops filled with fluid. Most jawed fish have three such loops too, and they work in the same way.
Dr Adjoa asks Kofi to turn around quickly three times and then stop. The room seems to swing, because the fluid in his ear loops keeps moving after his body has stopped.
Fish have small stones in their inner ears that tilt as the head moves. These ear stones, called otoliths, grow in rings, and scientists can count the rings to estimate a fish's age.
The eyes of fish and people are built like small cameras, with a lens at the front and a retina at the back. Both kinds of eye have a blind spot where the nerves leave the eye.

Cones are the cells in the retina that see colour, and ancient fish had four kinds of them. Most mammals lost two kinds, probably because early mammals lived at night, but our primate ancestors gained a third kind again.

A wall of small glass bottles, each holding a different smell, stands at the end of the hall. Humans have about four hundred working smell genes, and many more that no longer work, a sign that some ancestors had keener noses.
On a long table, drawings of a fish fin and a human arm are coloured to match. In the fin, the bones follow a pattern: one large bone, then two, then many small ones.
Most fish today have fins held up by thin rays, like the ribs of a fan. A few fish, called lobe-finned fish, have fleshy fins with real bones inside, and they are on our side of the family tree.
In 1938, fishermen near South Africa caught a coelacanth, a lobe-finned fish that scientists thought had died out with the dinosaurs. Since then, more have been found alive in deep water.
Kofi squeezes his upper arm and feels one thick bone inside it. This is the humerus, and it matches the single large bone nearest the body in the fin.
Beyond the elbow, Kofi has two forearm bones, the radius and the ulna. When he turns his palm up and down, the two bones cross over each other.
Past the forearm comes a group of small wrist bones, then the long bones of the palm and the fingers. In the fin, a spread of many small bones sits in the same place.
The same bone pattern appears in the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the leg of a horse. They look different and do different jobs, but one plan lies beneath them all.
In a human embryo, the hand first appears as a small flat paddle. The fingers form later, when the cells in the gaps between them die away.
Some of the genes that help to shape fish fins also help to shape human hands. Scientists study them in zebrafish and mice, and the results suggest that the same toolkit was reused.

Nobody planned the hand in advance, Dr Adjoa says, and that is the clever part of the story. A fin became a hand through many small changes, and each one had to be useful, or at least harmless, to its owner.
In the Hall of Shores, a large model shows a river bank from about four hundred million years ago. This was the Devonian, which is sometimes called the Age of Fishes.
Long before any animal with a backbone, mosses and small plants had spread across the land. Insects, spiders and their relatives followed, so the shore already held food.
Back in the water, life was crowded and dangerous. Warm, shallow pools held little oxygen, and large hunters such as giant sea scorpions prowled in them.
The shore offered food, such as insects and other small animals, and perhaps fewer enemies. Scientists think that a fish able to spend a little time out of the water might therefore do well.
A lobe-finned fish with lungs could gulp air when the water was poor in oxygen. Strong fins would let it rest its body on the bottom of a shallow pool.
Some fish alive today can already move over mud. Mudskippers, which are not our relatives, use their strong front fins to crawl and hop, and they breathe through their skin and mouths.
Kofi asks why a fish would want to go on land. Dr Adjoa says that fish do not plan, but animals that cope well in a changing place tend to leave more young.
In some places, the rivers of that time rose in floods and then dried up again. Many fossils from this period have been found in rocks that were once rivers and floodplains.
None of this happened quickly, and nobody should picture a single bold fish. From the first fish with fleshy fins to the first animals with legs took many millions of years.
At the end of the shore display stands a heavy door marked Gallery of In-Betweens. Dr Adjoa grins at Kofi and says that the star of the afternoon is waiting inside.
Under a bright light stands a cast of Tiktaalik, a fossil animal about three hundred and seventy-five million years old. Its bones were found in the far north of Canada, in the Arctic.
The name Tiktaalik comes from Inuktitut, a language of the Arctic, and it means a large freshwater fish. It was chosen with the help of elders from the region where the fossils were found.
Tiktaalik had scales, fins and gills like a fish, and it could grow to be as long as a small crocodile. Its flat head, with eyes on top, looked more like a crocodile's.
Most fish cannot turn the head separately, because the head is joined to the shoulder by bone. Tiktaalik had no such bones, so it could move its head from side to side.
With a neck, an animal can look around and snap at prey without moving its whole body. That helps a hunter in shallow water, and it helps even more on land.
Tiktaalik's front fins were strong, with a shoulder, an elbow and a joint like a wrist. They could bend, so the animal could probably push its body up out of the mud.
Tiktaalik had broad, strong ribs, like those of a land animal. In the shallows, they helped to support its body, which weighs much more out of water than in it.
Tiktaalik had gills for breathing in water, and probably lungs for gulping air. Large openings on top of its head, called spiracles, may have helped it to take in air.

Tiktaalik is called an in-between animal because it has features of both fish and early four-legged animals. Dr Adjoa says it is probably a close cousin of our ancestors rather than a direct ancestor.
Kofi holds his neck stiff and tries to look at a picture on the wall. He has to turn his whole body, and he decides that Tiktaalik had a very good idea.
Next to Tiktaalik stands Acanthostega, an animal from Greenland about three hundred and sixty-five million years old. It had real fingers, and yet it also kept its gills.
Nearby stands Ichthyostega, another early four-legged animal from Greenland. It had seven toes on each back foot, and its strong ribs and limbs may have let it drag itself across the mud.
Early tetrapods had six, seven or even eight fingers on each limb. Later, five became the usual number, and all of their descendants have five or fewer.
Acanthostega's limbs were too weak to hold up its body on land. Scientists think that it used them to paddle and to push through weedy water.
In 2010, scientists reported tracks in rock in Poland that are nearly four hundred million years old. They look like the footprints of an animal with four limbs, and they are older than Tiktaalik.
These tracks do not mean that Tiktaalik was wrong or unimportant. They show that the family tree is more like a bush with many branches than like a single straight line.
A cast of the Polish tracks lies in a glass case at the height of a child. Kofi places his hand beside one print and sees a row of small toe marks, like his own.
Fish have small hip bones, but a land animal needs strong ones to carry its weight. In early four-legged animals the hips grew bigger and joined firmly to the backbone.

Tetrapod means four feet, but the name covers every animal that descends from the first four-limbed ones. Frogs, birds and people are tetrapods, and so are snakes, which lost their legs, and whales, which returned to the sea.
Kofi asks whether this means that he is a fish. Dr Adjoa says that, on the family tree, he is a kind of bony fish, just as a sparrow is a kind of dinosaur.
In the Gene Gallery, Dr Adjoa explains that a gene is a short piece of DNA that works like a recipe. Cells read the recipes to build and run a body.
A set of genes called Hox genes lays out the body from head to tail. They do this job in flies, in fish and in people.
In a laboratory, a small change in one Hox gene can make a fruit fly grow legs where its antennae should be. The gene has sent the wrong instruction to part of the head.
A gene is useless unless something switches it on at the right time and place. Many differences between animals come from changes in these switches, not in the genes themselves.
In a corner of the gallery stands a tank of zebrafish, small striped fish no longer than a finger. About seven in ten human genes have a counterpart in the zebrafish.
A zebrafish embryo is almost see-through, so scientists can watch its heart beat and its nerves grow in a living animal. By switching off one gene at a time, they learn what each gene does.
A gene called Pax6 helps to build eyes in flies, fish and people. Strangely, the eye of a fly is built very differently from a human eye.
Scientists call this a toolkit: a set of old genes used again and again. Different animals use the same tools in different ways, and so they end up with very different bodies.
Because so many genes are shared, studies of fish, flies and mice can help scientists to understand human bodies. Some of what we know about health began with these small animals.
DNA changes at a slow, fairly steady pace, so the differences between two animals can act like a clock. Scientists check this clock against the fossils, and the two often agree.
In the Hall of Amphibians, a frog sits on a lily pad while a tadpole wriggles in the water below. The word amphibian means double life, because these animals live both in water and on land.
A tadpole breathes with gills and swims with a tail, like a small fish. As it grows, it develops lungs and legs, loses its tail and becomes a frog.

Frogs also breathe through their thin, moist skin, which can take in oxygen from the air or the water. Because the skin must stay wet to work, most amphibians have to live near water or in damp places.
Frog eggs are soft and covered in jelly, with no hard shell. They would dry out on land, so frogs return to the water to lay them.
Look at the side of a frog's head, behind the eye, and you will see a round disc of skin. This is the eardrum, and it picks up sounds from the air.
The next big step was an egg with a tough shell. Inside it, the baby is surrounded by membranes that hold water and food, so the egg can be laid on dry land.
One of those membranes is the amnion, a bag filled with watery fluid. A human baby grows inside an amnion too, floating in a little pond of its own.
The yolk sac is another old part of the egg. In a human embryo it is small and holds no real yolk, but it still helps to make the first blood cells.
Reptiles have dry, scaly skin that keeps water in, and their lungs are better at taking in air. With such bodies they could live far from the water.
Early on, the first amniotes split into two great branches. One branch led to reptiles and birds, and the other led to mammals, our own group.
The next room is the Hall of Mammal Cousins, and it is full of skulls with sharp teeth. These animals lived more than two hundred million years ago, and they were relatives of the first mammals.
A reptile has a lower jaw made of several bones joined together. A mammal has a lower jaw of just one bone on each side.
In a reptile, the jaw hinge is formed by two small bones at the back of the jaw and the skull. In a mammal, the hinge is made by different bones.
In some fossils of mammal cousins, there are two jaw hinges side by side. One is the old reptile hinge, and the other is the new mammal hinge.
Mammals have three tiny bones in the middle ear, called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. Together they carry the shaking of the eardrum to the inner ear.
The hammer and the anvil are the old hinge bones of the reptile jaw. In the ancestors of mammals they shrank, moved into the ear and took on a new job.
Small, light ear bones are good at passing on high sounds. Scientists think that the new hinge made the jaw stronger, and that the freed bones then became very good at hearing.
In a human embryo, the hammer and the anvil first form in the first arch, near the jaw. Later they separate and move to their place in the ear.
Kofi touches his ear and learns that the stirrup inside it is the smallest bone in his body. It is no bigger than a grain of rice, and yet it helps him to hear every word.
Only mammals have hair and make milk, and these features began in their early ancestors. A mother mammal feeds her young with milk made in her own body.
The air in the museum is cool, and Kofi's arms suddenly break out in goosebumps. Dr Adjoa asks him to look closely at the tiny bumps and at the hairs standing up from each one.
Each hair has a tiny muscle that can pull it upright, and that makes the skin bump. In furry animals this fluffs up the fur, which traps warm air or makes the animal look bigger.
Kofi tries to wiggle his ears and finds that he can, a little. Dr Adjoa says that the small ear muscles are left from ancestors that turned their ears towards sounds.
Dr Adjoa shows Kofi how to press his thumb and little finger together and bend his wrist. A thin cord stands up in the middle of the wrist, but about one person in seven has no such cord.
Early in pregnancy, a human embryo has a small tail. It shrinks away, and only a small group of fused bones, the tailbone, is left behind.
Humans carry a broken copy of a gene that makes yolk, the food store inside an egg. It no longer works, and it is a trace of egg-laying ancestors.
If a gene is no longer needed, changes can build up in it without harming the animal. Over time it may stop working, but it stays in the DNA like an unused page.
Now Kofi's hiccups come back, as loud as before. Some scientists think that hiccups come from a reflex that helps tadpoles breathe with their gills, but no one has proved it.
Another clue is that unborn babies hiccup, from early in pregnancy. They do it long before they ever breathe air, so hiccups cannot be just a mistake made while breathing air.
Kofi asks, rather impatiently, which of the ideas is the right one. Dr Adjoa says that scientists still do not know, and that saying so is part of doing science honestly.
Kofi sits down on a bench and rubs his lower back, which is tired from a long afternoon of standing. Dr Adjoa smiles and says that standing upright has its own price.
In most mammals, the spine is like a bridge between the front and back legs. In people, the spine stands upright, so the bones of the lower back carry a heavy load.
Our hips and knees carry the whole weight of the body on two legs, so they take a lot of strain. Walking on two legs also left the hands free, and that was a great gift.
Many people have too little room in the jaw for their last teeth, called wisdom teeth. Scientists think that human jaws became shorter over time, while the number of teeth stayed the same.
For a long time, the appendix was called a useless leftover. Now some scientists think that it may store helpful gut bacteria, although the idea is still being tested.

In the 1800s, Ernst Haeckel drew embryos in a way that made them look more alike than they really are. Modern scientists have shown that early embryos do share features, but they do not replay the whole history of their ancestors.

Careful studies of real embryos suggest that many backbone animals look most alike at a middle stage. Before and after that stage they look more different, so the pattern is not a simple replay of the past.
People sometimes say that humans are the top of evolution, but that is a mistake. Every living animal has had the same long time to change, and each one fits its own way of life.
Every body is a bundle of compromises between strength, speed, size and cost. None of them is perfect, but each one works well enough to live and have young.
Light from the high windows has turned gold, and the afternoon is nearly over. Dr Adjoa checks her watch and says that there is one more room to visit.
The last room, beyond the Hall of Mammals, is the Tree Room, where a giant tree of backbone animals is drawn across a long wall. Its branches carry fish, frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Scientists built trees like this one from bones and fossils, and then they built them again from DNA. The two kinds of tree agree on most of the main branches.

At the end of one branch, a small label says, “You are here,” next to a drawing of a boy. Kofi follows the branches backwards, past a mouse, a lizard, a frog and a lungfish, all the way to the lamprey.
On a wall is a photograph of a scientist brushing dust from a fossil bone at a field camp. New fossils are still being found every year, and each one tests and improves the story.
A good scientific idea must be open to being proved wrong. If evolution were false, fossils would turn up in the wrong layers, such as mammals in very old rock, and so far none has.
Dr Adjoa opens her notebook and reads her three rules once more. Kofi can say them from memory: ask what a thing is, ask how we know, and say so when nobody is sure.
Kofi opens his hand wide and looks at his fingers in the golden light. He thinks of the fins, the bones and the fish that came before them.
As the museum empties, Dr Adjoa keeps her promise about the hiccups. We know that a hiccup is a reflex involving the diaphragm and the voice box, but we do not know its original purpose.
At the glass doors, Kofi notices that something is missing: his hiccups have stopped, as quietly as they began. Dr Adjoa laughs and says that science cannot take the credit.
Kofi's mother arrives, and he walks out into the evening with his head full of fish, bones and fossils. He now understands that his body is a living museum, with old pieces in new places.
C1C2: Kofi had been hiccuping since lunchtime, and by the time he reached the tall glass doors of the Museum of Natural History, each hic rang out like a small bell. His mother, who had promised to collect him at closing time, kissed the top of his head and wished him luck. Inside, a quiet marble hall was waiting, and Kofi had the unhappy feeling that it was about to hear a great deal from him.

Dr Adjoa, the fossil scientist who had offered to show him around, was waiting on the steps with a worn leather notebook under her arm. She listened to one more enormous hic, nodded as though a colleague had just made a good point, and announced that even a hiccup has a very old story hidden inside it. If he would follow her, she promised, they would spend the afternoon tracing the body he lives in back to its beginnings.

High above the entrance hall hung the skeleton of a great whale, its ribs curving like the timbers of an upturned ship. Dr Adjoa explained that every animal with a backbone, from this giant to a bat to the boy standing beneath it, is built on one shared plan. Such animals are called vertebrates, she said, and in a way the whole museum was a family album.

Kofi reached behind him and ran his fingers down the middle of his back, where a ridge of small bumps ran all the way from his neck to his waist. Each bump, Dr Adjoa told him, belongs to one of a stack of bones called vertebrae, which are piled one upon another and cushioned by soft discs. The whale above them was built on the very same plan, only on a far grander scale.

Kofi counted off the cures he had already tried: holding his breath, drinking water from the wrong side of the glass and swallowing a spoonful of sugar. None of them had worked, and Dr Adjoa said that this was hardly surprising, since nobody has found a cure that works for everyone. A hiccup, it seemed, took orders from nobody, however clever or determined that person might be.

On the museum map she drew a long winding line that began in the Fish Hall, passed through a dozen smaller rooms and ended in the Hall of Mammals. The halls were arranged by age, she explained, so a stroll from one end to the other would also be a journey forward through time.
