In a single afternoon they would cross more than five hundred million years of the story of life.

In her notebook Dr Adjoa had written three rules for the afternoon, and she read them aloud as solemnly as a judge. First, ask what a thing is; second, ask how anyone knows; third, say so plainly whenever nobody is sure. Kofi, who was fond of questions, agreed at once, although his agreement ended in a hiccup.

Kofi, who was convinced that no one could really explain a hiccup, offered Dr Adjoa a bet. She laughed, shook his hand and promised to come back to the question before closing time, though she warned him that science still had a few honest gaps in this particular story. The deal was fair, she said, because the gaps were part of the story too.

At the far end of the hall a bright sign pointed towards a wide staircase and promised the oldest animals in the museum. Dr Adjoa explained that the builders had planned the museum like a pile of rock layers, with the earliest creatures at the bottom and the most recent ones at the top. Going down the steps, in other words, would be going back in time, landing by landing.

Kofi followed her down the winding stairs, and each hiccup bounced off the cold stone walls and came back to him a moment later. The light turned a deep, watery blue, and the air seemed to grow older with every step. He had the odd feeling of leaving his own afternoon behind and walking, quite literally, into the past.

The first room they reached was the Hall of Clues, where Kofi pressed his nose against a cabinet crowded with rocks, bones, shells and a brass microscope. Dr Adjoa said that none of these things was valuable in itself, but that each was a witness to events nobody had seen. Scientists, she said, are a little like detectives who arrive long after the event and must make do with whatever was left behind.

The first kind of clue, she said, is the fossil: the bones, shells or footprints of a living thing, preserved in stone for millions of years. A fossil is a solid photograph of the past, although it is rarely a complete one, and it never shows colour or sound. Even so, it tells us what bodies were like long before there was anyone around to look at them.

The second kind of clue lies in living bodies, which can be compared part by part and bone by bone. When two animals share an unusual feature built to the same pattern, scientists suspect that they inherited it from a shared ancestor, much as two cousins might share a grandmother's nose. The more features two animals have in common, the closer their relationship is likely to be.

The third kind of clue comes from embryos, the earliest stages of a growing animal, which are tiny and strange and surprisingly informative. Watching how a body builds itself can reveal relationships that are well hidden in the finished adult. Many of the features Kofi would meet that afternoon, Dr Adjoa promised, first appear in the embryo as simple and unfamiliar shapes.

The fourth kind of clue is DNA, the long chemical instruction book that sits inside nearly every cell of every living thing. Parents copy it and pass it to their young, with occasional small changes, so the DNA of close relatives is more alike than that of distant ones. By comparing the books of different animals, scientists can work out who is closely related to whom.

Kofi, who liked to see things for himself, asked whether anybody had ever actually watched evolution happen. Dr Adjoa answered by leading him to a long shelf where finches and beetles of many different kinds stood in rows under bright lights. Each row, she said, was a lesson in how bodies can differ even within a single kind of animal.

Look closely at the beetles, Dr Adjoa said, and you will find that no two of them are exactly alike, whether in size, in colour or in the shape of their legs. Some of these differences are inherited, passed down from parents to young through DNA, and that inheritance is where the whole process begins. Kofi thought of his own nose, which was exactly like his father's, and which his mother said had arrived without asking.

Some inherited differences give an animal a small advantage, such as a better way of finding food or of escaping an enemy. Animals with such an advantage tend to survive and to leave more young than their neighbours, and so the helpful difference becomes more common in the next generation. Repeated over a very long time, Dr Adjoa said, this slow sorting can reshape a whole kind of animal.

On a small island in the Galápagos, scientists once measured finches through a long drought, when the soft seeds ran out and only hard, tough ones remained. The birds with larger beaks could crack them, so more of those birds survived, and the next generation had beaks that were a little bigger on average. It was evolution caught in the act, though only a small step taken over only a few years.

Dr Adjoa warned Kofi that evolution has neither a goal nor a designer: it works only with the parts that already exist, changing them a little at a time. A body is therefore less like a brand new machine and more like an old house that has been extended, patched and rewired over the ages. Kofi hiccuped again and wondered, hopefully, whether his hiccups might be one of the patches.

In the Hall of Time, behind a rope, lay a slab of rock that had been split cleanly in two, and on its face was the pale outline of a small fish. Every fin and every scale had been caught in the stone, as though the animal had stopped for a portrait and never moved on. Dr Adjoa said that it had been swimming about long before the first human being was born.

When a fish dies and sinks into soft mud, its body may be buried before scavengers can destroy it. The soft parts usually rot away, but minerals dissolved in water can seep slowly into the bones and harden them, while the mud around them turns to rock. After millions of years the result is a fossil, which is partly bone and partly stone.

Becoming a fossil is extremely rare, because most animals are eaten, broken up or simply rot away without leaving a trace. This means that the fossil record is full of gaps, and every fossil we have is a lucky survivor from an enormous and unrecorded crowd. Dr Adjoa said that the gaps should not worry anyone, because the real surprise is that we have so many pieces at all.

Rivers and seas lay down mud and sand in flat layers, each new one settling on top of the last, so that a cliff may hold a very long record of time. Usually the oldest layer lies at the bottom and the youngest at the top, in the way that the oldest newspaper lies at the bottom of a pile. A fossil's depth, therefore, gives scientists a first rough clue about its age, to be checked by other methods.

Sometimes the movements of the Earth tilt layers on their sides, fold them like a carpet or even turn them upside down. Scientists therefore study each cliff with great care before they trust it, because the rule that the oldest layer lies at the bottom is usually true but never automatically so. Good science, Dr Adjoa remarked, is largely a habit of checking rules that seem obvious.

Some kinds of shellfish lived for a limited time yet spread over a wide area of ancient seas, which makes their shells excellent time markers. When the same kind turns up in rocks hundreds of kilometres apart, geologists can match the layers and conclude that they formed at about the same time. A fossil can therefore be a label for a moment as well as a creature.

Certain atoms in rock are radioactive, which means they change into other kinds of atom at a steady and well-measured rate that ordinary heat and pressure do not alter. The time taken for half of a batch to change is called its half-life, and for some atoms it is millions of years. By measuring how much of each kind is present, scientists can read the rock like a very slow clock.

Volcanoes throw out ash that settles in a layer and contains atoms that can be dated, so an ash layer works like a stamp on the rock record. A fossil found between two such layers must be younger than the lower stamp and older than the upper one, which gives scientists a bracket of years. The method is careful, repeated and cross-checked, and its results have agreed with one another again and again.

Many different measurements agree that the Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and the oldest traces of life are probably more than three billion years old. That leaves an enormous stretch of time before the first animals with backbones, which appeared only in the later part of the story. Numbers like these are hard to feel, Dr Adjoa admitted, so she had brought something to help.

Dr Adjoa unrolled a long strip of cloth across the floor and explained that every step along it stood for a hundred million years. The whole story of animals with backbones fitted into the last five steps or so, and our own kind arrived at the very end, in a sliver no thicker than a coin. Kofi, who had been feeling rather important, found this strangely humbling, and for almost a minute he forgot to hiccup.

The first case in the Fish Hall held a glowing model of a sea from the Cambrian period, more than five hundred million years ago. Its waters were crowded with spiny, shelled and many-legged creatures, some of them so odd that they looked like the work of a careless inventor. Almost all of them, Dr Adjoa pointed out, had no backbone at all, and the very few that did were small and easy to miss.

Even today, the great majority of animal species have no backbone: they are the worms, snails, insects, spiders and jellyfish that fill the planet and run most of its ecosystems. Animals with a backbone are therefore a small branch on a very large tree, though it happens to be the branch that includes us. Kofi, who had always taken his spine rather for granted, felt a small and unexpected burst of pride.

Animals with backbones belong to a larger group called the chordates, and every chordate shows four signs at some stage of its life. These are a stiff rod called the notochord, a nerve cord running above it, a tail that extends beyond the gut, and a set of slits or folds in the throat. A human embryo has all four at some point, which Kofi found slightly alarming until she explained what they become.

In a tank of clean sand lived a lancelet, a thin, see-through animal a few centimetres long that spends most of its life half buried on the seabed. It has a stiff rod and a nerve cord along its back but no true backbone, so it gives us a living hint of how the first vertebrates may have begun. Lancelets are not our ancestors, Dr Adjoa warned, but they are distant cousins that kept some very old habits.

Rocks at Chengjiang in China have given up fossils of soft-bodied animals that are about five hundred and twenty million years old, preserved in astonishing detail. A few of them are tiny and fish-like, with eyes, gills and zigzag blocks of swimming muscle, and some scientists think that they are among the first animals with backbones. Others argue about exactly where they belong, and Dr Adjoa was careful to say that the debate is still open.

A backbone does several jobs at once, Dr Adjoa said, and the first of them is to shield the delicate nerve cord that runs through it. It also gives the muscles a firm line to pull against, and it lets the body bend smoothly from side to side as the animal swims. Each of these gifts is enormously useful to a swimmer, which probably helps to explain why the design was kept.

Kofi bent forward to touch his toes and felt every part of his back curve and stretch, because each vertebra moves just a little against its neighbour. Dr Adjoa told him that his neck contains seven such bones, which is also true of a giraffe, whose enormous neck is made of seven very long ones. A pattern that works, it seems, tends to be kept and stretched and not thrown away.

At the front end of the backbone sits the skull, a tough case that protects the brain, the eyes and the other delicate organs of the head. Kofi knocked gently on his own forehead and felt the hard bone just beneath the skin. In the earliest fish the skull was probably made of cartilage and not of bone, Dr Adjoa said, but the job was exactly the same.

The first fish had no jaws at all, only a simple round mouth that sucked up or filtered tiny scraps of food from the water and mud. Some of them were armoured with heavy plates of bone, which suggests that the seas of that time were not safe places for a slow swimmer. In the Fish Hall, their stony heads stared out of the glass like the helmets of very small knights.

In a tank at the end of the hall, a lamprey clung to the glass by its round, toothed mouth, an eel-like fish that has never grown jaws. Dr Adjoa was careful to say that lampreys are not our ancestors but our cousins, since they have been evolving for exactly as long as we have. Still, because their bodies are built on a plan like that of the earliest vertebrates, they offer a good living hint of what those animals were like.

In the next room a fish skeleton and a human skeleton had been placed side by side, and Kofi walked slowly from one to the other. Both had a skull at the front, a spine down the middle and ribs that curved around the body, as if one plan had been drawn twice with different pens. The differences were real, Dr Adjoa said, but it was the similarities, hidden beneath them, that told the story.

A fish breathes by passing water over its gills, thin and feathery organs that absorb the oxygen dissolved in the water. Each gill is supported by a curved bar of bone or cartilage called a gill arch, and a row of these arches lines each side of the throat like the ribs of a small boat. Hold on to that image, Dr Adjoa said, because those bars are about to become very important.

Each arch, Dr Adjoa explained, is a small kit of parts built to a standard pattern. It holds a bar of cartilage or bone for support, a muscle to move it, a nerve to control that muscle and a blood vessel to feed the gill. Because the kit is repeated all the way along the head, evolution can alter one set while the others carry on with their old work.

Imagine a street of identical houses, Dr Adjoa said, in which one family decides to knock down a wall and build a grand new kitchen. The other houses carry on as before, so the street as a whole suffers no loss, and the experiment can succeed or fail without much risk. Repeated parts in a body give evolution exactly this kind of freedom, and it has used it again and again.

At some point in the distant past, scientists think, the front gill arches of certain fish grew larger and developed a hinge in the middle. Over a very long time those bars turned into jaws, a pair of levers that could open wide and snap shut. It was one of the most important changes in the history of vertebrates, and it began with a piece of a breathing frame.

With jaws, a fish could do far more than suck or filter its meals: it could seize, bite, tear and crush. That opened up a whole menu of new foods, from hard-shelled animals to other fish, and jawed fish spread through the seas and rivers in great variety. Today almost all vertebrates have jaws, and the lamprey is one of the very few exceptions.

Above the doorway hung a cast of the head of Dunkleosteus, an armoured fish that lived about three hundred and seventy million years ago and grew several metres long. Instead of teeth, its jaws bore sharp edges of bone, and they could probably have sliced through the armour of other fish. Dr Adjoa said that Kofi was looking at what a gill arch can become, given enough time.

Kofi opened and closed his mouth several times, with one finger resting just in front of his ear, and felt a small joint sliding beneath the skin. That joint is the hinge of his own jaw, a lever that has been used for chewing, talking, yawning and grinning. Dr Adjoa said that the hinge was a very old design, and that it sat close to the ear for a reason that would soon become clear.

In a human embryo the same plan is followed, with the first arch building the lower jaw and helping to shape the upper one. The arches behind it contribute to the bones of the ear and to the cartilage and muscles of the throat. These parts look quite different in the finished body, yet they all began as a row of similar folds, and Kofi swallowed and felt his throat with new respect.

Kofi yawned so widely that his ears popped, and for a moment the whole hall sounded a little clearer. Dr Adjoa explained that the popping comes from a narrow tube joining the ear to the back of the throat, a tube that is built from the same part of the embryo as the first gill slit of a fish. In sharks that slit stays open as a small breathing hole called a spiracle, but in us it became a path for air to reach the ear, a story that she promised to finish later.

In the next case the jaw of a great shark gaped wide, showing row behind row of triangular teeth, each as sharp as a kitchen knife. Beside it lay a small square of shark skin that visitors were invited to touch, and Kofi discovered that it felt rough, like a sheet of sandpaper. Dr Adjoa asked him to remember that roughness, because the teeth and the skin were secretly related.

Shark skin is covered with denticles, which are tiny pointed scales set close together like the tiles of a roof. Under a microscope each one has a hard glassy coat, a core of bone-like material and a soft centre that holds a nerve and a blood vessel. Dr Adjoa invited Kofi to compare that list with the inside of a tooth, and he realised that it was almost identical.

Many scientists think that teeth began as tough scales in the skin, and that at some stage in the history of jawed fish some of those scales spread into the mouth. There they were shaped, enlarged and sharpened until they became the biting teeth we know. The evidence lies partly in fossils and partly in the matching structure, and Dr Adjoa said that the idea remains the best explanation we have.

A shark's teeth are arranged in several rows, and the back rows keep moving forward like a slow conveyor belt to replace any teeth that break or fall out. Over its lifetime, a single shark may get through many thousands of teeth, so it never has to worry about wearing them out. Kofi, who had a dental check-up coming, sighed and said that he would happily swap.

Kofi pulled back his lip to show Dr Adjoa the gap where a baby tooth had fallen out only the week before. Humans, like most mammals, get just two sets of teeth, a small first set and a larger second set, so the second has to last for a whole lifetime. A shark would find that arrangement alarmingly thrifty, Dr Adjoa said, and perhaps a little unfair.

The glassy coat on the outside of a tooth is called enamel, and it is the hardest material in the human body, harder than bone and able to resist years of chewing. Unlike a shark's tooth, however, it cannot be replaced, and once it is worn away or damaged it does not grow back. That is one reason, said Dr Adjoa with a smile, why brushing is a very sensible habit.

In a nearby case hung the skeleton of a shark, a pale grey frame that looked as if it had been carved from rubber. It is made of cartilage, a firm and flexible material that is lighter than bone, which suits a fast and agile swimmer. Beside it stood a stiff white skeleton from a bony fish, and the contrast was obvious at a glance.

Kofi bent the rim of his ear and pressed the tip of his nose, and both sprang back into shape. Those parts of the body are made of cartilage, the same kind of tissue that forms a shark's entire skeleton, and it also cushions the ends of our bones where they meet at the joints. We have not lost cartilage, Dr Adjoa said, only given it a smaller job.

Much of every human skeleton begins as soft cartilage, and in a baby a great deal of it has not yet turned into bone. During childhood the cartilage is slowly replaced by bone, and many small bones fuse together, which is why an adult has about two hundred and six bones while a baby has rather more separate pieces. Growing up, Dr Adjoa said, is partly a matter of turning soft material into hard, one slow step at a time.

Jawed fish divided long ago into two great branches: the sharks and their relatives, with skeletons of cartilage, and the bony fish, with skeletons of bone. Every land vertebrate, from frogs to Kofi, descends from a bony fish, which is why we stand on the bony side of the family tree. The shark, then, is a distant cousin that took a different road, and not a lesser relative.

A short corridor led to the Hall of Beginnings, where a glowing model showed a human embryo only a few weeks old, curled like a comma and smaller than a bean. Along its neck ran a row of small folds, the arches, which looked like the ridges of a miniature accordion. Dr Adjoa said that they were among the most important clues in the whole museum.

Dr Adjoa was quick to explain that these folds are not gills and that the embryo never breathes with them, since it receives its oxygen from its mother's blood through the umbilical cord. Instead, the folds grow and change, and over the following weeks they become parts of the jaw, the ear, the throat and the neck. They are better described as a starting kit than as a fish still hidden inside the child.

Kofi asked, with some alarm, whether he had once possessed a set of gills, and Dr Adjoa laughed so loudly that a guard looked round the door. What he had had, she said, were the same starting parts that a fish uses to build its gills, but his body used them for something quite different. It is a little like using the same bricks to build a bridge or a garage.

The face, Dr Adjoa said, is not made in one piece but is assembled from several separate pieces of tissue, some of them from the arches, which grow towards one another in the embryo. They meet and fuse in the middle in a careful sequence, rather like the two sides of a zip. The little groove between the nose and the lip is a reminder of that meeting.

Hidden behind the arches in the model was the heart, which is one of the first organs to start working in an embryo. It begins as a plain tube, and it starts to pulse when the embryo is only a few weeks old, long before it has the shape of a heart. Kofi put a hand on his chest and felt his own heart going, steady and cheerful, unlike his hiccups.

Over the following weeks the tube bends, loops back on itself and begins to grow internal walls, which divide it into separate chambers with valves between them. By birth the result is a four-chambered heart, with two chambers on the left and two on the right, working as a pair of linked pumps. Nobody would guess from the finished organ that it had started as a simple tube.

Along the wall stood three glass models of hearts, each one more complicated than the last. A fish heart has two chambers, a frog heart has three, and the hearts of mammals and birds have four, so the series looks almost like a ladder. Dr Adjoa cautioned him that it is not a ladder, since every living animal has had exactly as long as we have to evolve.

A heart with four chambers keeps blood that is rich in oxygen separate from blood that has already delivered its oxygen to the body. This allows the organs to receive a strong supply, which suits warm-blooded animals such as mammals and birds, because they burn a great deal of energy to keep warm. It is a clever improvement, but it was built on the same tube that fish still use, with some extra walls.

In a fish, large blood vessels run through each gill arch, carrying blood to the gills to pick up oxygen. A human embryo begins by building the same pattern of vessels, and then it rebuilds them: some disappear, while others grow into the great arteries of the neck, the heart and the lungs. Evolution, Dr Adjoa observed, is a very thrifty renovator, and it seldom throws a useful pipe away.

None of this means that a human embryo passes through a fish stage and a frog stage on its way to becoming a baby. It follows a growth recipe that has been altered a little at a time over countless generations, and changes made to the earliest steps of a recipe tend to ruin the whole dish. That is why so many ancient steps are still there, quietly doing their work.

On the wall hung a diagram of a fish's head, with a bright line for each nerve running out of the brain and into the gill arches. Humans have twelve pairs of nerves that leave the brain, Dr Adjoa said, and several of them still follow the routes that were first laid down in fish. The map of our heads, in other words, was drawn long before there were any people in it.

In a fish, each gill arch has its own nerve, lined up from the front of the head to the back, and in a person the same lineup remains. The nerve of the first arch moves the jaw and gives feeling to the face, the next works the muscles of the face, and those farther back serve the throat and the voice. If a nerve is a telephone line, Dr Adjoa said, then the old exchange is still in use, and the numbers have barely changed.

Kofi smiled, frowned and raised one eyebrow at his reflection in the glass of a case, testing each expression as though he had just been given a new face. The muscles that produce them grow from the second arch, and in a fish the muscles of the same arch help to work the gill covers. Every smile he had ever given, Dr Adjoa said, was powered by a very old part.

One nerve in the head makes a far longer journey than all the others. It is called the vagus, a Latin word meaning wandering, and it leaves the brain, passes through the neck and fans out to serve the throat, the heart, the lungs and much of the gut. In a fish the same nerve serves the hindmost gill arches, and it seems to have wandered farther as the body changed.

Beside a giraffe skeleton, a diagram showed a nerve to the voice box that appears to run the wrong way. Instead of going straight from the brain to the throat, it travels all the way down the neck into the chest, loops beneath a great blood vessel near the heart and then climbs back up to the voice box. In a giraffe, said Dr Adjoa, that is a journey of several metres to cover a distance of a few centimetres.

In a fish the nerve took the shortest possible path, running straight to the last gill arch and passing close beside a blood vessel on the way. As the neck lengthened and the heart sank lower in the body over countless generations, the nerve stayed hooked around the vessel and was simply stretched, longer and longer, with each change. Evolution makes no plans to tidy up, Dr Adjoa said, and a small change that works is always easier than a redesign.

A human engineer would have taken the nerve straight to the voice box, Dr Adjoa said, but a changing body is not an engineering project. At every stage the living animals had to survive and breed with the nerve they already had, and each tiny stretch of the detour was easier than rerouting the whole thing. The result is a path that makes little sense as a design, but a great deal of sense as a history.

Kofi has the same arrangement inside his own neck, though in a person the detour is not very long. On the left side, the nerve to his voice box dips down into his chest, hooks under the great artery that leaves the heart and climbs back up again. Every word he speaks depends on that very old loop, and when he said hello, rather nervously, the nerve did its job exactly as it always had.

The diaphragm is the sheet of muscle that pulls air into the lungs, and Kofi was surprised to learn that its nerve begins high up in the neck. In the early embryo, Dr Adjoa explained, the diaphragm starts to form close to the neck, and as the body grows it moves down into the chest, taking its nerve along behind it like a dog on a long lead. The long path of the phrenic nerve is therefore a memory of where the muscle began.

At that very moment Kofi hiccuped again, loudly enough to make a passing guard jump. Dr Adjoa explained that each hic is a sudden jerk of the diaphragm, a breath that begins and is then cut off as the voice box snaps shut. Nerves in the neck and chest carry the signals in this reflex, she added, which means that Kofi's hiccups were running along some very old wiring.

Further along the Fish Hall, a glowing diagram showed a pair of lungs tucked inside the body of an ancient fish. Scientists think that lungs first appeared in early bony fish, long before any animal walked on land, and that they were at first a simple extra pouch for taking in air. Kofi, who had always assumed that lungs were a land-based invention, looked thoroughly surprised and then a little embarrassed.

Most bony fish alive today have a swim bladder, a gas-filled bag that lets them hover at any depth without having to swim all the time. Darwin was one of the first to suggest that this organ is a descendant of the old lungs, and later research has largely supported the idea. In a sense, the fish took a breathing organ and turned it into a buoyancy tank.

In the next tank swam a bichir, an African river fish with an eel-like shape, a row of small fins along its back and a pair of simple lungs as well as its gills. Every few minutes it rose to the surface and gulped a mouthful of air, then sank again as calmly as if nothing remarkable had happened. It is a living reminder of how an early bony fish might have lived.

In a murky pool at the back of the Fish Hall floated a lungfish, a living species that breathes air through true lungs as well as through gills. When its river dries up, an African lungfish digs into the mud, curls up in a little burrow and survives for months until the rains return, breathing air the whole time. Dr Adjoa said that such a creature shows how the first step towards land may have been small and practical.

Warm, shallow water holds little dissolved oxygen, and a stagnant pool with many fish in it can run short of oxygen on a hot day. Air, in contrast, is full of it, so a fish that could gulp air at the surface had a way to survive where its neighbours struggled. Lungs, Dr Adjoa said, were probably not a step towards land but a way of staying alive in bad water.

In a human embryo the lungs begin as a small bud that grows out from the front of the throat tube, the same tube that carries food towards the stomach. The bud divides again and again, forming a tree of branching airways, and it keeps on branching until a vast number of tiny endings has formed. It is a strangely thrifty way to make an organ, and it leaves a mark on the way we swallow.

Because the lungs grew out of the throat, the path of the air crosses the path of the food, and for a short stretch behind the mouth the two share a single passage. When we swallow, a flap called the epiglottis folds down over the windpipe, which usually works, but now and then a crumb takes the wrong turn and sets off a fit of coughing. Kofi remembered a sandwich that had done exactly that, and agreed that the design was not perfect.

Inside Kofi's chest, the branching tubes end in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, each wrapped in a net of very thin blood vessels. If their thin walls could be spread out flat, they would cover an area much larger than a bedroom floor, which gives oxygen a huge surface through which to pass into the blood. The fish's simple pouch, Dr Adjoa said, had become something rather grand, although the idea behind it was still the same.

At the top of the windpipe, the voice box can snap shut like a door to keep water and food out of the lungs. An animal that breathes air while living in or near water needs a reliable guard of this kind, Dr Adjoa said, and the first lungfish would have needed one very early. Kofi suspected that she was coming to the hiccups and asked her to hurry.

Kofi took a long, deep breath, filled his lungs to the top and held it while Dr Adjoa counted slowly to ten. The hiccups vanished for a few glorious seconds, and then, with a sound like a small door slamming, they returned as loudly as before. Dr Adjoa patted his shoulder and told him that they still had a long way to go and that the best parts of the story were yet to come.

Along each side of a fish's body, if you look carefully, runs a faint line of tiny pores. This is the lateral line, a sensing organ that lets the fish feel movement and pressure in the water around it, so that it can notice a predator, a meal or a neighbouring fish even in the dark. It is a kind of touch that works at a distance, Dr Adjoa said, and humans have nothing quite like it.

Under each pore sit hair cells, each carrying a bundle of microscopic hairs that sway when the water around them moves. The bending of the hairs opens tiny gates in the cell, and the cell sends an electrical signal along a nerve to the brain. The whole system is a beautifully simple device for turning motion into information, and the same trick turns up again in our own ears.

A school of fish can wheel and turn as if it were a single animal, and part of the secret is that each fish feels the movements of its neighbours through its lateral line. Sharks and many other predators use the same sense to detect struggling prey in murky water or at night, long before they can see it. A fish listens to the sea with its skin as well as with its ears, and the two senses are cousins.

Deep inside the human ear, protected by a very dense bone, there are hair cells of the same basic kind. Here they detect the tiny shakes of sound and also the movements of the head, signals that we use for hearing and for balance. Fish, amphibians and birds can regrow these cells when they are damaged, Dr Adjoa added, but mammals, to our great loss, mostly cannot.

Above the hearing part of the inner ear sit three tiny loops filled with fluid, each one lying in a different direction, like three hoops set at right angles. When the head turns, the fluid inside the loops lags behind and bends the hairs, which tells the brain which way the head is moving. Almost all jawed fish have the same three loops, laid out in much the same way, which suggests that the design has been hard to improve.

Dr Adjoa challenged Kofi to turn on the spot three times, as fast as he could, and then stop dead. The whole hall seemed to swing around him, because the fluid in his ear loops kept moving for a few seconds after his body had come to rest. He staggered, laughed and noticed with surprise that for the entire spin he had not hiccuped even once.

Fish also have small stones inside their ears, called otoliths, which rest on beds of hair cells and tilt when the head moves, telling the fish which way is down. They grow by adding thin layers, rather as a tree adds rings, and scientists can count the layers to estimate how old a fish was when it died. Humans carry tiny crystals of a similar kind in the balance organs of their own ears, doing much the same job as the fish's stones.

The eyes of fish and humans are built to the same camera-like plan, with a lens at the front to focus the light and a retina at the back to catch it. The plan has an odd flaw, however: the nerve fibres run in front of the light-sensing cells and leave through a hole that creates a small blind spot in each eye. An octopus has a camera eye too, but it evolved separately and is wired the other way round, so it has no blind spot at all.

Cones are the cells in the retina that detect colour, and the ancestors of land animals had four kinds of them, which gave them a rich view of the world. The early mammals, which probably lived in the dark, lost two of the four, and most mammals today see a more limited range of colours than a goldfish does. Some of our primate ancestors regained a third kind, thanks to a change in a gene, and that is why Kofi sees red apples and green leaves as different.

At the end of the hall stood a wall of small glass bottles, each holding a different smell, and Kofi worked his way along it with his nose. Humans have about four hundred working genes for smell receptors, and many hundreds more that no longer work, which suggests that some of our ancestors had a much keener sense of smell than ours. Kofi decided that the bottle labelled cheese was the one he trusted least, and that the bottle labelled rain was the one he liked best.

On a long table lay a drawing of a fish's fin beside a drawing of a human arm, and the bones in each had been painted in matching colours. In the fin, a single large bone sat nearest the body, two bones came after it, and then came a spread of many smaller ones, and the arm followed exactly the same sequence. Kofi looked from one to the other as though somebody had played a trick on him.

Most fish alive today have thin, flexible fins held up by slender rays, like the ribs of a paper fan. A small group, the lobe-finned fish, has fleshy, muscular fins with a core of real bones, and every land vertebrate descends from that group. Kofi was proud to learn that his family had once been the odd ones out.

In a corner of the hall hung a model of a coelacanth, a large lobe-finned fish that scientists believed had died out with the dinosaurs until one was pulled from the sea off South Africa in 1938. Since then more have been found living in deep water off the coasts of Africa and Indonesia, where they drift slowly among the rocks. Their fins are fleshy and move in an alternating pattern rather like the legs of a walking animal, which makes them especially interesting to anatomists.

Kofi squeezed his upper arm and felt a single thick bone beneath the muscle. This is the humerus, Dr Adjoa told him, and it is the descendant of the single large bone at the base of the lobe-finned fish's fin. A humerus is a lever and a hinge and a place to attach muscle, and it has been doing that work since long before anyone had a name for it.

Beyond the elbow come two bones side by side, the radius and the ulna, which correspond to the two bones that follow the single bone in the fin. Kofi turned his palm up and then down, and Dr Adjoa pointed out that the two bones were crossing and uncrossing under his skin like a pair of chopsticks being twirled. That clever twist is one of the things that lets us turn a doorknob, and it was not available to a fish.

Past the forearm comes a cluster of eight small wrist bones, then the long bones of the palm and, finally, the bones of the fingers, which number fourteen in each hand. Where the fin has its spread of many small bones, the hand has its own crowd, packed together in a way that allows the fine movements of writing, throwing and playing music. Kofi flexed his fingers and tried to imagine them as the stiff, fan-shaped end of a swimmer.

The same sequence of bones lies hidden in the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale, the leg of a horse and the digging paw of a mole. Kofi thought of the whale skeleton in the main hall and realised that its flipper hid a humerus, two forearm bones and a row of finger bones, like a hand inside a mitten. One plan, rebuilt for many purposes, was beginning to look like a theme of the whole museum.

Kofi's own hand, Dr Adjoa told him, began as a small flat paddle at the end of a tiny limb bud in the embryo, with no fingers at all. The fingers appear when the cells in the gaps between them receive a signal to die, a carefully controlled process that carves the paddle into separate digits. The same carving is used in many animals, though in ducks it stops sooner and leaves the webbing in place.

Some of the genes that shape fish fins also help to shape human hands, and experiments on zebrafish and mice have found that parts of the same genetic programme are at work in both. The details are still being worked out, and Dr Adjoa was careful to say so, but the broad picture is that the toolkit for building a limb was inherited and then adjusted. A fin did not vanish so that a hand could appear; the same toolkit was simply used in a new way.

Nobody planned the hand in advance, Dr Adjoa said, and that is the most important thing to remember about the whole story. A fin turned into a limb and a limb into a hand through countless small changes, each of which had to be useful, or at least harmless, to the animal that carried it. Kofi wriggled his fingers in the blue light and felt, for the first time, that they belonged to a very long family.

In the Hall of Shores, a long glass case held a model of a river bank as it looked about four hundred million years ago, in the period called the Devonian. The Devonian is sometimes known as the Age of Fishes, because so many new kinds appeared in its seas, rivers and lakes, from armoured giants to the first fish with fleshy fins. Beyond the water, the model showed something that Kofi had not expected, which was a green and very strange shore.

Long before any animal with a backbone set foot on a shore, mosses and low plants had spread across the land, and taller plants with real roots followed. Insects, spiders, millipedes and other small animals came after them, and by the Devonian the margins of rivers and lakes held a good deal of food, in the form of both leaves and creatures. The shore was empty of large animals, Dr Adjoa said, which made it a promising place for a newcomer.

Back in the water, life was crowded and dangerous, because the warm, shallow pools and river margins were full of fish competing for food and space. Oxygen was sometimes scarce, and large hunters, among them giant sea scorpions that could grow longer than a man, lurked in the murk. A fish that could slip away from such a place, even for a short while, might find itself with an advantage.

The shore offered a different bargain: a supply of insects and other small animals, plenty of sunlight and warmth, and perhaps fewer enemies than the crowded water. Scientists think that a fish able to spend a little time on the edge of the water, grabbing a meal or escaping a hunter, might therefore have done rather well. The move was probably less like a leap and more like a series of small, reluctant steps.

A lobe-finned fish with lungs could gulp air when the water ran short of oxygen, and one with strong, muscular fins could prop itself up on the bottom of a shallow pool to rest. These two abilities, a way to breathe air and a way to hold the body up, were already present in fish that never left the water. Dr Adjoa called them the keys that were lying on the table before anyone knew there was a door.

In a corner of the shore display, a short video showed a mudskipper, a small fish that spends much of its life out of the water on tidal mud flats. It props itself up on its strong front fins, crawls and hops across the mud and breathes partly through its skin and the lining of its mouth. Mudskippers are not our relatives, Dr Adjoa said, but they show that a fish can manage on land for a while without changing beyond recognition.

Kofi asked why on earth a fish would want to leave the water, and Dr Adjoa answered that wanting did not come into it. No animal chose to become a land animal, she said, but in each generation the ones that coped best with shallow, drying, crowded pools tended to leave the most young. After enough generations, the little advantages added up to a new way of life.

In some regions, the rivers of that age rose in seasonal floods and then shrank into scattered pools as the dry season returned. Many of the fossils from this period have been found in rocks that were once river channels and wet plains, which suggests that the first four-legged animals lived in just such places. A fish that could cross from one drying pool to the next had a great advantage over one that could not.

None of this happened in a hurry, and nobody should picture a single bold fish flopping out of a pond one fine morning. Between the first lobe-finned fish and the first animals with true legs lay tens of millions of years, a span that dwarfs the entire history of our own species. In that time countless generations lived and died, and each one passed on a body only a little different from the last.

At the end of the shore display stood a heavy wooden door with the words Gallery of In-Betweens painted above it in gold. Dr Adjoa grinned at Kofi, put her hand on the handle and said that the star of the afternoon was waiting inside. Kofi hiccuped, which he decided to take as a cheer, and followed her through the door.

Under a ring of bright lights stood a cast of Tiktaalik, a fossil animal about three hundred and seventy-five million years old, whose bones were found in the rocks of the Canadian Arctic. In its own time that region was warm and green, with rivers winding across a low plain, and nothing at all like the frozen place we know today. Kofi had read the name on the sign three times and was still not sure how to say it.

The name Tiktaalik comes from Inuktitut, a language spoken across the Arctic, and it means a large freshwater fish. It was chosen with the help of elders from Nunavut, the Canadian territory where the fossils were found, which seemed fitting for an animal that had lived in a river there so long ago. Dr Adjoa said it with a care that made Kofi try the word himself, and he got it right on his third hiccup.

Tiktaalik was a fish in many ways, with scales, fins and gills, and it grew to a length of perhaps two metres or more. Its flat, wedge-shaped head, with eyes set on top, looked much more like the head of a crocodile, and it suggests an animal that lay in the shallows with its eyes just above the water. Few creatures have ever combined so many surprises in so small a space, and Kofi found it hard to look away.

In most fish the head is joined to the shoulder girdle by a ring of bones, so the whole front of the body has to turn together. Tiktaalik had lost those bones, which gave it a true neck and, with it, the ability to turn its head on its own. For a hunter lying in the shallows, that small freedom was worth a great deal.

A neck is easy to take for granted, but it lets the head look, sniff and strike while the body stays still, so a hunter can stay hidden as it tracks its prey. On land, where an animal must watch for danger and pick food off the ground, the neck becomes even more useful. Almost every land vertebrate since, from frogs to humans, has inherited this useful trick.

The front fins of Tiktaalik were strong and bony, with a shoulder, an elbow and, most remarkably, a flexible joint that worked like a wrist. With such fins the animal could probably do a kind of push-up, lifting its chest clear of the mud so that it could breathe air and look around. Kofi, who was not good at push-ups, said that he found this deeply impressive.

Its ribs were broad and overlapping, far stronger than those of a typical fish, and they would have helped to support the body when it was lifted out of the water. In water a body is held up by the liquid around it, but in air it feels very heavy indeed, a fact that anyone who has climbed out of a swimming pool will recognise. Kofi, who had often struggled out of a swimming pool, recognised the feeling at once.

Tiktaalik kept its gills, which worked in the water, but it very probably had lungs as well, and the large openings on top of its head, the spiracles, may have helped it to gulp air at the surface. In warm, stagnant pools, such a double system would have been an excellent insurance, offering a second way to breathe whenever the first one failed. Dr Adjoa noted that the evidence for the lungs is indirect, which is a polite way of saying that nobody has found one.

Tiktaalik is often called an in-between animal because it mixes the features of fish with those of the earliest four-legged animals, and it fills a gap that scientists had long suspected must exist. Dr Adjoa was careful to say that it is probably a close cousin of our ancestors and not necessarily a direct ancestor, since the family tree has many branches and only a few have been found. It is not a missing link in a chain, she said, but a very good snapshot of a stage along the way.

Kofi held his neck perfectly stiff and tried to look at a painting on the far wall, which obliged him to swing his entire body round like a ship turning in a harbour. He did it twice, to be sure, and then he announced that the creature in the case had had a very good idea indeed. Dr Adjoa laughed and said that the neck was one of evolution's quiet triumphs, though it had done nothing at all for his hiccups.

Beside Tiktaalik stood the cast of Acanthostega, an animal from Greenland that lived about three hundred and sixty-five million years ago and had real limbs with real fingers. Yet it also kept gills, a fish's tail and a body that looked rather like a large, thick salamander, so it was still, in Dr Adjoa's words, a creature of two worlds. Kofi counted its fingers on the cast and found, to his astonishment, that there were eight on each front foot.

Nearby stood Ichthyostega, another early four-legged animal from the same part of Greenland, with seven toes on each hind foot and a heavy, strong set of ribs. It probably spent time dragging itself across mud and sandbanks, although its movements were perhaps more like those of a seal than a lizard. Dr Adjoa said that the museum's two Greenland casts were like first drafts of a very long book.

Early tetrapods experimented with the number of fingers and toes, and those that scientists have found had six, seven or eight on each limb. Later the pattern of five became the usual one among their descendants, and many animals lost some of them, as a horse has done, but none seem to have added new ones. Your own hand, with its five fingers, bears the marks of a pattern that was settled long ago and then kept.

A surprise awaited Kofi in the details of the skeleton, for the wrists and ankles of Acanthostega were too weak to carry its weight on dry land. Scientists think that it used its limbs underwater, to paddle, to steady itself and to pull its way through weeds and roots. The first legs, it seems, were not made for walking on land at all, and they were put to a new use only later on.

In 2010, scientists reported a set of tracks pressed into an ancient shoreline in Poland, and the rock that holds them is nearly four hundred million years old. The marks look like the footprints of an animal with four limbs, which would make them older than Tiktaalik by many millions of years, and that was a puzzle nobody had expected. Dr Adjoa said that some scientists still argue about what made the tracks, and that a good scientist can enjoy being puzzled.

The tracks did not make Tiktaalik wrong or unimportant, Dr Adjoa said, but they reminded everyone that the family tree is more like a bush than a ladder, with many branches growing at once. Some of those branches died out, some are still alive today, and fossils are always found in a lucky and scattered order. Each new discovery changes the picture a little, and the sensible response is to enjoy the change.

A cast of the Polish tracks lay in a low case, and Kofi, who had been told that he could touch the copy beside it, pressed his hand next to the biggest print. It showed a row of toe marks pressed into stone, and looking at them gave him a strange feeling, as though somebody had walked past only a moment before. Something with toes had walked here, Dr Adjoa said softly, and the stone had kept the news for almost four hundred million years.

Fish have only small hip bones, buried in the flesh, because water carries most of their weight. A land animal needs something stronger, and in the earliest four-legged animals the hips grew larger and, over time, became firmly attached to the backbone, forming a solid base for the hind legs. Kofi sat on a nearby bench with a new respect for his own hips, which had been holding him up since he first stood.

The word tetrapod means four feet, though the group includes every animal that descends from the first four-limbed ones, whether or not it still has four feet. Frogs, birds and people are tetrapods, and so are snakes, which lost their legs long ago, and whales, whose ancestors walked on land before returning to the sea. Evolution, Dr Adjoa said, is happy to move in any direction that works, and nothing in it is ever final.

Kofi asked, in a small voice, whether all this meant that he was a fish, and Dr Adjoa considered the question with great seriousness. On the family tree, she said, he belongs to the branch of the bony fish, just as a sparrow belongs to the branch of the dinosaurs, though nobody would mistake either of them for their ancestors. He was a fish that had learned to walk, she added, and he was still learning to stop hiccuping.

A short walk later they reached the Gene Gallery, a quiet room lined with glowing screens. A gene, Dr Adjoa explained, is a short stretch of DNA that works like a single recipe, and the cells of the body read those recipes to build the proteins that make up and run a living thing. A human being has about twenty thousand of them, Kofi was told, and he did not remember being consulted.

One famous set of genes, the Hox genes, acts a little like a foreman who tells each part of the embryo what it is going to be. They lay out the body from head to tail, and in flies, fish and people they do essentially the same job, even though a fly and a human being look nothing alike. Even more curiously, the genes sit along the DNA in the same order as the body parts they control.

In a famous case studied in laboratories, a small change in a single Hox gene caused a fruit fly to grow legs where its antennae should have been. The gene had, in effect, sent the wrong instruction to a part of the embryo, and the embryo had followed it faithfully. Such results show that a few master switches can have enormous effects on the shape of a body.

Genes need switches, short stretches of DNA that decide when and where a gene will be used, and a good deal of evolution seems to have happened in the switches and not in the genes themselves. Altering a switch can make the same recipe appear in a new place, at a new time or in a new amount, and the result may be a longer limb, a different colour or a changed beak. Dr Adjoa compared it to the conductor of an orchestra, who does not write the notes but decides when each one is played.

In one corner of the gallery stood a tank of zebrafish, small striped fish no longer than a finger, which swam in quick silver flashes. About seven in every ten human genes have a recognisable counterpart in the zebrafish, Dr Adjoa said, which is one reason why laboratories all over the world keep these tiny fish. Kofi asked whether the fish were relatives, and Dr Adjoa said that they were, though rather distant ones.

The embryo of a zebrafish is nearly transparent, so scientists can watch its heart beat, its blood flow and its nerves grow in a living animal under a microscope. By changing or switching off one gene at a time, they can discover what each gene is for, and then they can ask whether the human version does a similar job. Zebrafish are tiny, Dr Adjoa said, but they have taught us a great deal about how a backbone animal is built.

A gene called Pax6 helps to start the building of eyes in animals as different as flies, fish and people, even though a fly's eye is built on a different plan from ours. In one laboratory experiment, the version of the gene from a mouse made fruit flies grow extra eyes in odd places, such as on their legs, and the extra eyes were fly eyes and not mouse eyes. The gene was a master switch, it seems, and the animal supplied the instructions for the details.

Biologists often speak of a toolkit, meaning a collection of very old genes that animals use again and again to build bodies. Because so many of the tools are the same, an animal can change dramatically without having to invent anything new: it only has to use the old tools a little differently. This is a thrifty kind of creativity, Dr Adjoa said, and it makes the history of life look less like a series of inventions and more like a long exercise in remixing.

Because so many genes are shared, careful studies of fish, flies and mice can shed light on how human bodies work and sometimes on what goes wrong with them. A good deal of medical research begins with a small animal in a laboratory, Dr Adjoa said, and it works only because those animals really are our relatives. Kofi decided that the next time he saw a fly, he would nod politely.

Small accidental changes build up in DNA at a slow and fairly steady pace, so the number of differences between two animals can work as a rough clock that tells us when their lines split. The clock is never perfect, and scientists test it against dated fossils and adjust it with care, but its answers often agree well with what the rocks say. Two different kinds of evidence, one in stone and one in cells, can therefore tell a single story.

In the Hall of Amphibians, a frog sat on a lily pad while a tadpole wriggled in the water beneath it, and the museum had labelled them with a single word. Amphibian comes from a Greek word meaning a double life, and it fits animals that begin in water and end up, for the most part, on land. Kofi hiccuped at the frog, and the frog, which was made of plaster, did not reply.

A tadpole breathes with gills and swims with a flat tail, and for the first weeks of its life it looks and behaves like a very small fish. As it grows, it develops lungs and legs, absorbs its tail and changes the shape of its mouth and its gut, and it emerges from the water as a frog. Dr Adjoa said that few events in nature show a body being rebuilt so completely, and that one can watch it in any pond in spring.

Frogs and their relatives also breathe through their thin, moist skin, which can take in oxygen directly from the air or the water. Because the skin must stay damp to do this job, most amphibians have to live near water or in wet places, and they quickly come to harm in dry, hot air. Their bodies, in other words, still keep one foot in the pond, even when the rest of the frog is sitting on dry land.

Frog eggs are soft balls of jelly with no hard shell, and a clump of them in a pond looks rather like a handful of glass beads. Out of the water the eggs would quickly dry out and die, which is why frogs return to ponds and streams every year to lay them. This habit probably tied the earliest four-legged animals to the shoreline for a very long time.

Behind each eye of a frog, if you look closely at the model, you will see a flat round disc of skin, a little like a drum. This is the eardrum, which picks up sounds travelling through the air and passes the shaking along to the inner ear. Fish do not need one, Dr Adjoa said, because water carries sound straight through their bodies, and the problem of hearing in the air was one that evolution had to solve.

The next great step was a new kind of egg, in which a tough or leathery shell surrounds the embryo and several thin membranes hold in water and handle food and waste. Such an egg can be laid on dry ground without drying out, and the young that hatch from it need no pond at all. Animals that develop in eggs of this kind are called amniotes, and they include reptiles, birds and, through their ancestors, mammals.

One of those membranes is the amnion, a bag filled with watery fluid that surrounds the embryo and protects it, so that the young animal grows inside a small pond of its own. A human baby develops in an amnion too, floating in the fluid, even though a mammal that is born alive no longer needs a shell. Dr Adjoa smiled and said that every one of us began life inside a piece of very old egg design.

Another old part of the egg is the yolk sac, which in a bird or a reptile holds a store of food for the growing embryo. A human embryo has a yolk sac as well, but it is small and holds no real supply of yolk, and it takes on other jobs, including the making of the first blood cells. It is a clear example of a part that changed its work when the old work was no longer needed.

Reptiles have dry, scaly skin that keeps water inside the body, and their lungs have more folds in them than those of amphibians, which helps them to take in more air. With such features, and with eggs that did not need water, they could live far from any pond and spread across dry land. The first animals of this kind appeared more than three hundred million years ago, and their descendants eventually reached every continent.

Early in their history, the amniotes divided into two great branches that were never to meet again. One of them led to the reptiles and the birds, while the other led to the mammals, so our own line parted from the reptile line more than three hundred million years ago. Dr Adjoa led Kofi towards a dim doorway, beyond which the creatures on our side of that split were waiting.

The dim doorway led to the Hall of Mammal Cousins, a long room full of skulls with sharp and surprisingly varied teeth. The animals they belonged to lived hundreds of millions of years ago, before the first mammals appeared, and they stood on our side of the great split with the reptiles. A few of them looked rather like lizards, Dr Adjoa said, though they were not lizards at all.

On a table lay the skull of an early mammal relative, and Dr Adjoa pointed to its lower jaw, which was made of several separate bones joined by seams, as a reptile's still is. A mammal's lower jaw, by contrast, is a single bone on each side, and Kofi's own jaw, when he felt along it, was one solid piece. Where, then, had all the other bones gone, he wondered, and how had they not been missed?

In a reptile, the hinge of the jaw is formed where a small bone at the back of the lower jaw, the articular, meets a bone in the skull called the quadrate. In a mammal the hinge is made by quite different bones, and the old hinge bones are nowhere to be found in the jaw. Dr Adjoa let the mystery hang in the air for a moment before she resolved it.

The clue, she said, lay in fossils that caught the change in the act, because a few mammal cousins had two jaw hinges side by side. The old hinge used the articular and the quadrate, and the new one used the bones that mammals have today, so the animal could go on feeding itself without difficulty whichever joint it relied upon. That was the key to the whole transition, since no creature can afford a broken jaw while its design is being altered, and Kofi, who had never wanted one, saw the point at once.

Mammals have three tiny bones in the middle ear, named for their shapes the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup, and together they carry the shaking of the eardrum across the air-filled space to the inner ear. The stirrup, which is the smallest bone in the human body, is much older than the other two, and it is related to the single ear bone that a frog or a lizard has. The other two have a more surprising origin, as Dr Adjoa had been waiting to explain.

The hammer and the anvil, Dr Adjoa announced, are the old jaw-hinge bones of our reptile-like ancestors, the articular and the quadrate. In the line that led to mammals they grew smaller, moved into the ear and took on a new job, passing sound inwards instead of holding a jaw together. It is one of the best-documented changes in all of palaeontology, and Kofi felt that he ought to applaud.

Small, light bones are good at passing on quick vibrations, and many mammals can hear much higher sounds than reptiles can. Scientists think that the new jaw hinge made the bite stronger and steadier, while the old hinge bones, freed from the work of chewing, were able to specialise in hearing. Evolution, as Dr Adjoa liked to say, will happily use an old part for a new job if it happens to fit.

The embryo tells a similar story: in every human the hammer and the anvil begin to form in the first arch, close to the jaw, and later they separate from it and settle into the middle ear. A tiny rod of cartilage that once helped to build the lower jaw stays behind to guide the process, and then it mostly disappears. Dr Adjoa thought that the embryo remembers more than it lets on, which she found both funny and moving.

Kofi touched his ear and learned that somewhere behind the skin, in a cavity in the skull, three small bones were quietly doing their work. The stirrup, no bigger than a grain of rice, is the smallest bone in the whole human body, and yet it helps to carry every word and every hiccup to his brain. Kofi decided that he owed his hammer and anvil an apology for ever having ignored them.

Two more features set mammals apart: they have hair, and the mothers feed their young with milk. Both features began in the early ancestors of mammals, although fossils rarely preserve hair or milk glands, so scientists have to work out the details from clues such as tiny canals in skulls that may have carried nerves to whiskers. Milk, in particular, may have started as a watery fluid that kept soft eggs from drying out, a theory that Dr Adjoa described as interesting but not yet proved.

The air in this part of the museum was cool, and Kofi's arms suddenly broke out in goosebumps, which made him shiver and laugh at the same time. Dr Adjoa asked him to look closely at the tiny bumps and at the fine hairs standing up from each one, as though they had been summoned to attention. She said that he was looking at a reflex that was older than the first human being by a very long way.

At the base of each hair lies a tiny muscle that can pull it upright, and when the muscles tighten together the skin is dragged into little bumps. In a furry animal the same reflex fluffs up the coat, which traps a layer of warm air in the cold and makes a frightened animal look larger to an enemy. Human skin has so little hair that the reflex now achieves almost nothing, Dr Adjoa said, but it still switches on every time we are cold or startled.

Dr Adjoa challenged Kofi to wiggle his ears, and after a few grimaces he found that he could, very slightly, to the delight of a small child standing nearby. The muscles that do this are leftovers from ancestors that turned their ears towards sounds, as a cat or a horse still does, and in most people they are too weak to move the ear much. A part that has lost its main job, she said, often hangs around as a curiosity.

Dr Adjoa showed Kofi how to press his thumb and little finger together and bend his wrist, and a thin cord stood up in the middle, just beneath the skin. It is the tendon of a muscle called the palmaris longus, which may have helped climbing ancestors to grip, but about one person in seven has no such muscle at all, and it makes almost no difference to them. Kofi checked both wrists carefully and was relieved to find the cord on each.

Dr Adjoa mentioned a fact that she had not had time for in the Hall of Beginnings: early in pregnancy, every human embryo has a small tail, with a few more vertebrae than it will finally need. The tail shrinks and disappears within a few weeks, and the last few bones fuse into the tailbone, or coccyx, at the base of the spine. Kofi, who had never thought of himself as a creature that once had a tail, sat down rather carefully on his own coccyx.

Hidden in human DNA, Dr Adjoa said, lies a broken copy of a gene that in egg-laying animals makes the proteins of yolk, the food store in an egg. The gene no longer works, because our mammal ancestors stopped needing it when their young began to be fed in other ways, but its damaged remains are still there, like a recipe with the pages torn out. Egg-laying mammals, such as the platypus, still keep a working copy, which is just what we would expect if the gene was lost after our own line gave up laying eggs.

If a gene stops being useful, nothing prevents random changes from piling up in it, since an animal does not suffer when an unused recipe becomes unreadable. Over time such a gene may be broken beyond repair, yet it can remain in the DNA for millions of years, a fossil of a different kind. Human DNA is full of such remains, including hundreds of broken smell genes, and each one is a small piece of history written in code.

At last the conversation came back to Kofi's hiccups, which the cool air of the hall had not cured. Some scientists have suggested that hiccuping is the remains of an old reflex that helps tadpoles and other gill-breathing animals to pump water, closing the throat at just the right moment. Dr Adjoa was quick to say that nobody has proved this, and that the true reason for hiccups remains an open question.

Another clue comes from the womb, because unborn babies hiccup too, beginning early in pregnancy and long before they have ever breathed air. That fact is hard to explain if hiccups are only a mistake in breathing, and it has led to other ideas, such as clearing air from a feeding baby's stomach or exercising the breathing muscles. None of these ideas is firmly established, Dr Adjoa said, and she gave Kofi a look which suggested that he was free to invent another.

Kofi asked, with some impatience, which of the ideas was the right one, and Dr Adjoa answered that nobody yet knows, which is a perfectly respectable thing for a scientist to say. What scientists do know is that a hiccup is a reflex, a loop of nerves that a full stomach, a fizzy drink or a gulp of air can set off, and that the loop is probably very old. Why the loop exists at all is a question still waiting for a good answer.

By now Kofi had been on his feet for hours, and he sat down on a bench with a sigh, rubbing his lower back with one hand. Dr Adjoa sat beside him and remarked that his tired back was another part of the story, because walking upright is one of the most unusual things a mammal can do. Standing on two legs has brought us great gifts, she said, but it has also brought us a few bills.

In most mammals the spine works like a long arched bridge, held up at each end by a pair of legs, with the organs hung beneath it. When our ancestors began to stand upright, the same spine had to be stacked on end like a pile of coins, and it developed gentle S-shaped curves that help to spring and balance the weight. The design works well, but the lower back carries a heavy load, and it is a common place for aches.

On four legs the weight of the body is shared among four limbs, but on two legs the whole load passes through the hips, the knees and the feet, which take great strain over a lifetime. Against that cost stands a very large benefit, because walking upright left the hands free to carry food, to hold babies and, much later, to make tools and hold pencils. Evolution, said Dr Adjoa, is full of such bargains, and nobody gets all the advantages for free.

Many people find that there is not enough room in the jaw for the last of their teeth, the wisdom teeth, which push through late and sometimes at awkward angles. Scientists think that the human jaw became shorter over a long period, perhaps as our diet and our tools changed, while our teeth did not shrink to match. The result is a mismatch between two parts that evolved at different speeds, and Kofi ran his tongue over his teeth and decided to think about something else.

For a long time the appendix, a small pouch attached to the gut, was described as a useless leftover of a plant-eating ancestor. More recently, some scientists have suggested that it may serve as a safe house for helpful gut bacteria, and studies show that something like an appendix seems to have evolved more than once in mammals. Dr Adjoa pointed out that this was a good reminder to be careful with the word useless, since a part can seem pointless until someone finds its job.

In the nineteenth century, a German scientist named Ernst Haeckel published drawings of embryos that exaggerated their similarity, and he claimed that each animal re-enacts its ancestors' history as it develops. Later scientists showed that his drawings were misleading and his idea was wrong, and yet the early stages of embryos do share real features, such as the neck arches, which reflect the common ancestry. Careful modern research thus keeps what is true, discards what is not and keeps checking both.

Careful studies of real embryos suggest that many animals with backbones look most alike at one middle stage of development, when the neck arches, the tail and the first nerves are all in place. Before that stage and after it they differ much more, and the pattern is more like an hourglass than a ladder, although scientists are still debating how strong the effect really is. The honest answer, Dr Adjoa said, is that embryos carry real traces of ancestry, but that they do not replay it like a film.

People sometimes talk as if evolution were a ladder with humans at the top, but Dr Adjoa said that the picture is quite wrong. Every living animal has had exactly as long as we have to change since our shared ancestors, and each one is well suited to its own way of life, whether that is hunting in the dark or filtering the sea. A lamprey is not an unfinished person, and a person is not a lamprey that has made good.

Every body is a bundle of compromises between strength, speed, size and cost, and none of them is perfect in the way a drawing on paper can be. What evolution produces is not the best imaginable body but one that works well enough for the animal to survive and leave young, and then to be tinkered with again by the next generation. Seen like that, Dr Adjoa said, the strange leftovers are not embarrassing flaws but fascinating evidence of how the job was done.

High above them the windows had turned a deep gold, which told Kofi that the afternoon was slipping towards evening, and the hall was growing quiet as visitors drifted towards the exit. Dr Adjoa looked at her watch, closed her notebook with a decisive snap and announced that there was one room left, the one she liked best of all. Kofi hiccuped, stood up from the bench and followed her, and he noticed that his back already felt better.

The last room, beyond the Hall of Mammals, was the Tree Room, and its whole length was taken up by a great branching tree, painted in soft colours and lit from above like a stage. Along the branches sat fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals, and at every fork a small label named the ancestor that all the animals beyond it shared. Dr Adjoa stood back and said that the tree was the whole afternoon in a single picture.

Scientists first drew trees like this one by comparing bones and fossils, and in recent decades they have drawn them again by comparing the DNA of living animals. The two methods are completely independent, so it is striking that they agree about nearly all of the main branches, and the places where they disagree are the subject of lively and useful argument. A story told by stone and by cells at the same time, Dr Adjoa said, is a story worth trusting.

At the tip of one small branch Kofi found a label that read, “You are here,” beside a drawing of a boy with his hand raised in a wave. He traced the line back with a finger, past the mouse, the lizard, the frog and the lungfish, through the shark and on to the lamprey. Every fork reminded him of something from the afternoon, whether the lungs, the neck, the jaw or the ear, and it was a strange and wonderful thing to be shown the address of his own body.

On the wall hung a large photograph of a scientist kneeling in a dry valley, brushing dust from a fossil bone with a soft brush while the sun beat down. Every year new fossils like it are found, and every one of them tests the story and sometimes forces a change in it, which is exactly what a healthy science should expect. Dr Adjoa said that she had been wrong about several things in her career and that each time had been a small celebration.

A good scientific idea must be open to being proved wrong, Dr Adjoa said, and the story of the fish inside us has been open to that test for well over a century. If it were mistaken, fossils would keep turning up in the wrong layers, such as mammals in rocks that were laid down before any land animals existed, and the DNA of living animals would refuse to fit the tree. So far neither has happened, though scientists go on looking, because looking is the whole point.

Dr Adjoa opened her notebook at the page of rules and asked Kofi whether he could remember them, and to her surprise he recited all three without a mistake. Ask what a thing is, ask how we know, and say so when nobody is sure: he had used each one a dozen times since they had come down the stairs. It occurred to her that Kofi had become, over a single afternoon, a rather good scientist.

Kofi held up his hand in the golden light of the window and opened it as wide as it would go, and for the first time in his life he really looked at it. He pictured the single bone of the upper arm, the two bones of the forearm and the little bones of the wrist beneath the skin, and behind them a fin in the shallows of a Devonian river. His hand was not just his own, he realised, but the latest page in a very long book.

As the museum emptied, Dr Adjoa kept her promise about the bet, and Kofi listened carefully. A hiccup, she said, is a reflex in which the diaphragm jerks and the voice box snaps shut, run by nerves whose paths were laid down in our fish ancestors. Why the reflex exists is still uncertain, she added, and Kofi decided that an honest answer of that kind was worth more than a confident wrong one.

At the tall glass doors, with the sun sinking behind the trees, Kofi noticed that something was missing, and it took him a moment to realise that it was the hiccups. They had stopped as quietly and as mysteriously as they had begun, and neither he nor Dr Adjoa could say exactly when. She laughed and said that science could take no credit at all, and that she had never been so pleased to be left with an unsolved problem.

Kofi's mother arrived exactly at closing time, and he ran down the steps to meet her, so full of questions that she hardly knew where to begin. Behind him the great glass doors swung shut on the Tree Room and a kind scientist waving from the lobby, and ahead lay the ordinary evening, with its ordinary streetlights and its ordinary noise. Yet he walked into it with a new feeling, for he knew now that his own body was a living museum, and that every jaw, ear, hand and breath he carried had a story that began in the sea.
